product_title: Canon PowerShot A1400 16.0 MP Digital Camera with 5x Digital Image Stabilized Zoom 28mm Wide-Angle Lens and 720p HD Video Recording (Black) (OLD MODEL)
review_body: GREAT LITTLE CAMERA! The lens is sharp, focus is fast and accurate. The optical finder is FANTASTIC when working in situations where the LCD screen is difficult to see. I had several other point and shoots before which had screens that made shooting almost guesswork, as you so often could not see the screen, even with a flip out hood on it. With this, I hardly ever look at the screen, as the finder works so well, it zooms right along with the LCD image. The only time the finder is not good is for closeups inside a couple of feet or so, because it is not through the lens, but rather a "tunnel" finder, meaning that while it works with the lens, the viewing is through a finder tunnel. Thus, at the very close distances, there is parallax error. So, when shooting at close distances, I just go back to using the screen. This camera is also very small, easily goes into a jacket pocket, pants pocket, even some shirt pockets. It also will use AA batteries, instead of something which has to be charged. Of course, if you prefer, you can buy rechargeable AAs and a charger, but if you are caught out somewhere, you can use regular AAs. Lithium type are preferable on the AAs, but alkaline will work, also. If using alkaline AAs, especially with flash, battery life may be a bit short. This accepts SD cards, so no problem with storage on it. You can vary file size (MP), I prefer to keep it at 16MP, and I have 20"x30" prints on my wall which are pretty sharp at that level. Video on this is adequate, as is sound, for a point and shoot. On video and sound, though, keep in mind that this is a tiny point and shoot camera, and should not be compared with DSLRs which cost 5-10 times and much and are also bigger and heavier. For a still camera, I don't think you could do much better in a point and shoot!

review_body:
Beware of the gray market Hikvision cameras that are actually the Chinese version with English firmware updated. I tried to download the latest official firmware from Hikvision and load it, bricked all of the cameras. Then I found out that most of the cameras being sold are gray market, not us or international editions. Only those official editions support the official hikvision USA firmware.

Apparently, two ways to identify the "proper" cameras that get official firmware updates are either:

1)Red/White box (if you get the camera shipped in a brown box, it's very likely that it's Chinese).
2) If the serial number contains CCCH then you've gotten a gray market version. CCWR should be updatable from Hikvisions official firmware sources.

There is a whole community devoted to hacking the cheaper Chinese versions of these cameras, but I couldn't make it go in a few hours and I'm a pretty knowledgeable person. Good luck, the camera is fine, but get one that supports the official firmware & gets upgrades!

product_title: Arlo Smart Home - 1 HD Camera Security System
review_body:
Installation and setup was very easy. I created my account and it found the base station, and the view from the camera was live on the web page. There was a slight delay, but that is understandable. I installed the app on my Android phone without any problems.

Next day I tried to go to the website to play around with some settings, but it said that the base was not connected. It was sitting right next to me with all green lights. I power cycled it anyway, but that didn't make any difference. I was using IE11 for my browser. I switched to Chrome, and it worked. I went back to IE and it still said it was disconnected. I tried my phone and it worked fine. I went back to Chrome, and now that failed too. It seems like it only works on the android phone, but not on my computer. I Googled the error message and there are a lot of people having the same problem.

I bought this set for my parents who live in Pakistan. I asked them to try it from there. It is even worse from there. The login screen doesn't even load for them. Needless to say, I will be returning this and research some other security cameras. One star for the easy installation and setup.

review_body: I received the Smatree suction cup mount which came in a real small box. I was surprised on how well it folds down in such a compact way that it would not take as much room. The suction cup part performs exactly like the gopro branded one, in that you press the center button on the mount while bringing the lever down to lock it onto a smooth surface. This mount is different than the gopro brand because it has an extra pivoting head. I was able to tighten all thumb screws to prevent any movement and was satisfied that it would move while filming. Although I do suggest for any brand mount outside a vehicle to use a leash or tether just in case it loses suction. I usually use an old shoe lace cut very short and tie it some where to stay secure and not flap around in the wind. If you are going to use it on any glass I also suggest a good cleaning of the glass to get the best grip. I really like this mount and think it is a great alternative to paying double if not triple for the name brand product. I was given a sample product in return of my fair and honest review.

product_title: FLIR FX Dash/Sports Bundle Wireless 1080P HD Video Monitoring Security Camera
review_body:
This camera is really incredible. This is my second one (the first one wasn’t purchased on amazon).
Starting from unpacking and install - the setup process was super easy, clean and intuitive. It’s hard to believe there are people here that had trouble with this, and I assume they just had slow internet or some other unrelated problem.

The first use of the app was also amazing. Took me about 5 minutes to understand each and every feature. The only thing I had a bit trouble finding is the “smartzone” setting button (it’s near the motion detection sensitivity settings), and even this was pretty easy to find.

Basically, it has all I could ask for in terms of home security:
- Local memory card to store recordings
- Cloud storage that saves recordings and events, so if god forbid someone broke in the apartment and stole the camera, I still can access the cloud recordings
- Motion detection
- Night vision
- Battery This is so important! Sometimes the power dis for few seconds and cameras with no internal battery just die or reset!)
- Intuitive app with live streaming from ANYWHERE! (Seriously, I’ve logged to my home camera from so many different places around the world I think I broke a record)
- Two way radio (This is just fun to use, nothing more than this)

I Hope this is useful.

product_title: Panasonic LUMIX DMC-CM1 Camera Smartphone, 1" 20MP Sensor, Leica DC Lens, 4.7-Inch LCD (Black)
review_body:
I picked up my CM1 last year while in Germany and figured I'd try it for a few months here in the States and flip it if I wasn't that thrilled with the phone or felt the camera wasn't that great... needless to say, I have kept the camera and love it. this is now my only smart phone that I use.

For anyone who says this isn't any better than an iPhone, they obvouosly have never used the CM1, the difference is substantiial and having access to RAW files makes this a camera that I can actually use creatively. In addition, I now have access to Aperture, Shutter and ISO controls so I have total control of the image. Speaking of apperture controls, I can even now get a shallow depth of field as long as the subject is close... something that I could never do with my smart phone.

Before I got this phone, my walk around camera was a Sony RX100MKII, that camera has not been used in months, most of my snap-shots are now being taken with the CM1 and when I want to get really creative or need top notch quality I use my A6000.

As for the phone, I have no issues thus far. I just updated the handset to Lollipop and the phone is great. I am a T-Mobile user and it is great to get a break on my monthly service because I own the handset (of course for $1000, I better get a discounted service plan) and I like that Panasonic didn't give the phone a stupid skin or tons of bloatware that I would never use. This phone is very close to a pure Android experience with the exception of the camera app and the timelapse app, but these are great and where really needed given the features that this camera offers.

I have added some pictures so you can see the results, I am a happy camper and will keep this as my phone for a long time... at least until Panasonic ore someone offers a better camera in their phone than this one.

product_title: Nikon COOLPIX S9700
review_body:
Caveats!
1) Battery life can be a real problem. I bought a spare battery, but read on...
2) If you try to charge the battery with an auto recharger, it actually DRAINS the battery! I tried this with several auto charging cords and adapters, as well as a portable backcountry charger, and each time this happened. Huge disappointment when I realized this during a weeklong backcountry trek in Yosemite, when both my batteries drained after about 30 pictures. Really was left high and dry in a spectacular setting.
3) The flash does pop up at awkward times, as many reviews state, when in your pocket. Huge product design flaw. I don't use the flash that much but I could see how popping open in a pocket or backpack could easily break off this mechanism.

In terms of picture quality, I find it to be a bit better than the iPhone 6, but considering the flaws mentioned above, not enough to warrant the additional expense, in hindsight.

product_title: Andoer Caden K1 Waterproof Fashion Casual DSLR Camera Bag Case Messenger Shoulder Bag for Canon Nikon Sony Army Green
review_body:
Just received. Plenty of room in the main compartment. Very customizable. 3 removable, padded, velcroed (small, med, and large) dividers. The fabric feels like a heavy nylonish canvas. Stitching looks solid. Pockets galore. Netting, straps, click buckles, cinchers, and velcro/elastic-strap organizers on the long straps. If I had to guess, someone in the military designed this. It reminds me of a cross between a RUK sack, and the gas mask carrying case. Wearing it is self explanatory, but you will have zero confidence that you are wearing it correctly. Use the pictures in the Amazon item description to reinforce that you are wearing it correctly.

I have a Samsung camera kit; it came with a Samsung Galaxy Tab GT-P3110. I have two lenses...18-55m, and a 50-200m, couple caps, memory cards and charging cables. It all fits with plenty to spare. I would say there is still room enough for a sizable lens, about the size of a 12 oz can of soda, maybe larger depending how you organize the bag.

Zippers look solid too. You can ratchet the whole bag together when you are traveling, or leave some of the straps unclicked and just use the quick access zippers to get at your camera quickly. Either way it would appear everything will still be really secure. Also, the perimeter of the bag is padded on all sides, plus the additional padding of the dividers I mentioned should enable all your equipment to be well secured. If you have a tablet for reviewing photos, it can fit in an outer pocket, less protected, or on the inside with the camera and two lenses in a well padded environment. There is also a rain fly that is separate, and kept in the compartment that rides against your body. Think of a shower cap that would fit over an NFL helmet, with an additional strap to secure it to the bag.

Time will tell if the stitching holds up, but as of right now it looks solidly built. I could see this surviving a Lewis and Clark expedition or a summit of Mt. Everest. I am very pleased with the purchase. This is under priced in my opinion. I feel like it deserves 5 stars. Maybe I will change it after some time spent with the product.

review_body: [[VIDEOID:3b20fd5a9d0c0f25b45d4de571175d47]]I held off writing a review until I used this to shoot a wedding.  I loved this device and gave it a 4 stare review. It was amassing for the first 1 3/4 weddings. During the dance of the 2nd wedding I smelt something getting hot. I reached over and pickup my camera and this battery back was hot. One of the integrated circuits shorted out and put a full drain/draw on the batteries. The batteries where so hot that they started to melt the plastic of the Duracell batteries. The IC was so hot it started to melt the case. Their is no on off switch on this battery pack thankfully this happened while I was using it, what would have happened if I put the camera in my car and this happened on my drive home? I also uploaded a video and photo.  This is like having a second gas tank for your car, not like having a turbocharger or nitrous kit on your car. What I mean is that using this battery back my flash will recharge / recycle about 1 second faster after a “full discharge” Than it will recharge / recycle with ought the battery back. This battery pack allows me to shoot for a longer time without the recharge / recycle time slowing down as the batteries start to go dead. If you need fast recycle time after a full discharge look at "Quantum Turbo Power Packs" available on Amazon. They run at a higher voltage.  I did have to use a wood chisel to remove some of the plastic in the battery holder. It was keeping the battery from making contact with the terminal. Never good to hear I had to use a wood chisel to fix my brand-new photo gear. But hay this thing is under $30. Many reviewers complained it was difficult to insert the plug into the speed light but mine worked perfectly.

product_title: Photogenic StudioMax III 320ws Constant Color Monolight with Reflector
review_body:
There are several reasons that I did not like these lights, and ended up returning them.
First, the housing unit for the light was made out of plastic, and the way you attach a softbox or beauty dish, it was just like a slide in at the top, with a simple screw to keep the speedring attached. It just seems so flimsy and cheap...though the lights themselves, are not cheap-well at least compared to Alien Bees.

Second, the lights were not consistently firing. When you own a portrait studio, you cannot afford to have inconsistent lighting! The item must work, consistently, each and every time. I had a PPA Master Photographer come over to my studio, to help troubleshoot the lights, and everything we tried was tied right back to the lights, themselves. We tested to make sure it wasn't the studio electricity, the cords, the transceivers, and we even made sure to make sure it wasn't a bad hotshoe on the camera. All of that was tested. The only time the main light would fire is if I was using a cord, instead of using the Wireless. Even doing that, the fill light (which was acting as a slave) would not fire consistently.

NO MORE LOOKING THROUGH PINHOLES
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Okay, when I was I kid, my dad bought us an optical telescope with . It was fatiguing to use because the greater the magnification, the smaller is the opening in the eyepiece AND the less light there is. Worst of all, you see your own eyelashes quite a bit.

With this, once the software is installed, you can place anything under it and capture steady video images. No slides need. And no getting your own eyelashes in the way.

Not super high resolutions, but still -- all things considered, far better than what I could see in the microscope I had when I was growing up. At the same time, it's not too much of a shock in that I can capture similar images using my Nikon p600 in macro mode...although not at the level of magnification this microscope can reach.

review_body:
I am the student master of audio and lighting at my high school. I am also in charge of communications systems in my school auditorium, so, when we needed to be able to view the stage in the pitch dark when the props were moving on and off the stage between acts, we turned to these affordable and amazing little devices. I paired two of these units together with my wireless Uniden security camera which has horrible night vision (about 10 feet). The infrared lights were hung up on our fly-reel system about 16 feet off the ground, and the camera was mounted to a wall on stage right between to legs (side curtains) giving us about a 10x60 foot view of our stage. The two lights lit up that whole area perfectly during complete darkness. The spread on this light is minimal (about 45 degrees) , but it reflects very well onto other objects allowing my lighting technician to see the stage crew. I could not be happier with both of these lights, however, I have only had them for two weeks so I'll update this review in a year. I also plan to add a photo soon.

Some closing statements:
These lights are small but very powerful
Very affordable
They will only show up on cameras built for night vision(make sure it can pick up IR LED Wavelength 850nm)
This IR light has a photo sensor, so they only light up when it is dark
The light does NOT come with a plug so make sure you buy the right kind ( DC 12V 500mA) using the wrong plug will damage the product
I DO NOT HAVE THESE UNITS PLUGED IN 24/7

product_title: Olympus TG-4 Waterproof Digital Camera
review_body:
I am not an experienced photographer whatsoever, but I have recently become interested in at least understanding the basic concepts and the art of photography. I have done a lot of research and have a decent understanding of camera controls and how changing certain settings controls exposure or focus. I bought this camera as a (relatively) inexpensive way to get started with basic photography, but also as a way to get some beach/underwater shots, as those places are a common vacation spots. This is one of the best waterproof cameras out there and it makes for a decent point and shoot as well. I did a lot of research on underwater cameras and this was clearly the best option available.

First use was at a concert that I played in. Gave it to a (non-photographer) friend who took pictures during the show. I think I could have gotten a couple better pics if I had control of the settings during set. It took OK pics. Nothing all that great, but nothing worse than you'd find in most point and shoot cameras. It's very difficult to capture good concert photos without a nice DSLR where you can go manual and have full control over the shot, as the lighting usually fools the camera. In solid lighting, the TG-4 takes pretty good pictures.

Took it to the beach over the weekend and it held up well. It rained the whole time, but I still got some decent pictures on the beach. So it survived the rain as well as the pool and ocean. The lens did fog up when it started raining (due to the cold rain mixed with the humid air) but it did clear up after about 15 minutes. That is to be expected with these cameras and is a common issue. The ocean here on the east coast is brown so no underwater ocean pics, but I got some really nice shots in the pool. Clear pics and good colors. No internal leakage or any issues with the toughness. I was very careful to lock the doors on the camera securely beforehand and follow the procedures to rinse the camera and open it in the correct way after it dried. If you're using it in or around the water a lot, I'd recommend getting a floating strap (I got the Nordic Flash strap, it does the job well) as it will save it in case you happen to drop it. I shot mostly in aperture priority mode and got some good shots. I manually adjusted the exposure compensation and ISO setting as it was various degrees of cloudy throughout the day. FYI, shutter speed is automatically set. You can fiddle with the other important settings (ISO, Fstop, exposure compensation, etc) to change it, but you cannot manually control the setting. It's got a pretty fast shutter speed (up to 1/2000) in decent light and with the right settings, however.

I got some really cool shots at night with the live composite mode; I would definitely recommend trying that one out on a tripod. Get creative.

I'm going to Hawaii later this year and am looking forward to seeing what this camera can do in the crystal clear waters there. So far, this has been an investment/product that has been definitely worth the purchase.

review_body:

It's almost always connected, but sometimes has to be reset, maybe 1 or 2 times a year. It's been outside all the time, mounted just under the eve of the house, with a cord connection cover on the plug, that's tucked up even higher and out of the weather. We live in Central California, which gets in the 100°+ and low 30°'s during the course of the year. I've used Windows 7, 8, & now 10, with no problems.
Yes, it's more for the experienced, or techy types, that are willing to trial & error it till it works with whatever s/w you want to setup for your IP cams, & yes, it works with IP cam software, you do need to know the settings, which aren't always going to jump in your face, you have to know how to find the correct settings. (I never used the Foscam s/w, it just didn't find the camera :/ ) Get "Advanced IP Scanner" free s/w to 'find' your IP address at least. You have to login to the camera s/w to set the rest, like please at least setup/change the password.
Overall, I'd get Foscam again, would like a HD one next time, with better night time video, as I set it up when we leave to record video. Otherwise, it sends pics whenever there is movement. Love that feature. :)

product_title: Ubertronix Strike Finder Pro with MCDC2 Cable for Nikon Cameras (Lightning, Laser, Time Lapse)
review_body:
I purchased this one year ago almost to the date of this writing.
Overall, I'm not liking the quality. It's very light weight, plastic box with a couple of buttons and a dial on it. Knob on the dial fell off immediately and won't stay on. I almost sent the unit back because of it. Maybe some glue..but why glue something you spent $170 on!?? Now it's lost somewhere.
So now you have to wait for a storm...so I waited....and waited. You never have it when you need it. Packed it away until this weekend when the remnants of Erika were coming through. Thunderstorm warnings, good time to finally use it!!
First attempt was exciting. It does capture the lighting flash, YOU just have to make sure you're pointed in the right area. It takes some practice- but it worked! YAY!!
Second attempt the intervalometer dial broke, turns all the way around without stopping or setting time. I have no idea if it even works. Do I need it? Probably not but why spend this much on something that's going to break on second use? Disappointment is setting in.
Third attempt. Sigh.... Braved the elements, set up in a safe location. Lighting was in the distance, I was excited. I captured one lightning strike and then...my camera wouldn't shut off!! 30 pictures snapped before I knew what was happening. Turned off the camera, turned off the SFP....waited. Turned it on, everything ok. Another lightning strike in the area set it off and another 18 snaps of nothing. Maybe the battery is dying?? I replaced the battery. Reset....and it started freaking out all by itself. Grrr! Storm moved off. Pack up, go home to write this rant.
I can't tell you how disappointed I am.
I do have emails out to the company, lets see if they respond. If it's favorable, I will change my rating because I really want this to work!!

product_title: Meade ETX 80AT 80mm Altazimuth Refractor Telescope with Autostar Computer Controller
review_body: My Review:  I started in astronomy in June 2015 with inexpensive 10X50 binoculars.  I really liked the wide views.  I spent about 2 months using binoculars, a planisphere, “Turn Left at Orion” and various internet tools.  I joined two astronomy forums.  In August I decided I wanted to expand my glass.  The decision I had to make was, should I get 15X70 binoculars or would I go for my first scope?  After reading a LOT on the forums I decided I wanted a short FL refractor that could give me similar low power wide views to larger binoculars but would also give me stable views, Goto and the ability to go up in magnification.  The ETX 80 seemed to meet that criteria.  The included 26 mm Meade Super Plossil eyepiece provides a 15X 3.4 degree field of view which is very binocular like in feel.  I use this eyepiece more than any other.  The included 9.7 mm eyepiece provides 41X and relatively wide 1.3 degree view.  I have since added a Meade Super Plossil 6.4 mm eyepiece for 62X.  When combined with the built in 2X barlow this gives me 15x, 30x 41x, 62x, 82x and 124x. That is a pretty nice range of magnifications.  Views of the moon, Saturn and stars were very good.  I observed a number of Messier star clusters and Deep space targets such as the Andromeda Galaxy, the butterfly cluster and others.  I split the double star Alberio and found the “coat hanger”.  These all looked great in the wide views provided by the ETX 80.  I later added external 2X and 3X barlows which took my top magnification to 186X which I have used on Saturn and the moon.  Overall I would say anything over 150X is only useful on very bright objects.  For most objects I find I typically observe at under 100X.  High magnification is not that the strong suite for this telescope but even in my larger scope, which I purchased later, I do most of my observations at 150 X or less.  Some people don’t like the focuser as it is a fine tuning focuser.  I understand their concern but I don't find it an issue.  By design this is a fine adjustment focuser so it is slow if you want to make a large range focus adjustment as would be needed when using the internal flip barlow.  However once you are in the general focus range of you eyepieces the amount you need to turn to go to a different eyepiece is quite small and you can really fine tune the focus.  I think it works well.  The internal barlow works fine but, as noted above, you have to turn the focuser a LOT when using it.  It is better than nothing but an external barlow is more convenient.  I later picked up separate 2X and 3X barlows which I can also use with other telescopes.  This has eliminated this focuser issue.  Refocusing with these is quite easy. But the flip barlow is always there if I want a barlow and don’t have the external ones with me.  My skies have very few stars and some areas have no visible stars at all, so GoTo was important to me.  The GoTo has been quite good and accurate once I trained the drives, as described in the manual.  However I noticed that running it on the internal 6 AA batteries only provides about 5-6 hours of useful life, especially in cooler temperatures.  Then the scope gets slow and I start to get drive failure issues.  I actually returned the first ETX 80 for drive fault errors as I thought it was the drives.  I now believe the first scope may have been fine and the issue was low batteries.  I have since purchased a car adapter cable and now I can plug it into a power port in the car or run it off a car jump start pack.  This works GREAT! The slews, the moving of the scope from target to target, are fast and no more drive fault issues.  I highly recommend this $12-$20 accessory cable.  I love the GoTo but I also want to learn to star hop the way one would do with a manual scope.  I like that I can release the clutches and use the scope manually.  I later learned that not all GoTo scopes allow this.  I use the ETX 80 manually about 50% of the time.  I bought a Telrad finder scope for it but have not installed it. I tend to do my star hopping with binoculars then target the scope using a $5 green laser mounted on the telescope with rubber bands.  This works extremely well.  Looking through the 26 mm/15X  eyepiece is like looking through the finder scope on many other telescopes so I find I really don't need a separate finder scope.  I really enjoy the portability.  All up it is about 12 pounds.  It lives in the garage with my accessory box.  I can scoop it up with the accessories, walk to my observation site, set up and observing manually in 5 minutes.  If I want to use the GoTo add another 5 minutes.  The ETX 80 is so easy to toss in the car for quick hops.  I love it!  I have not used it as a table top, off the tripod, but it is good to know I can leave the tripod home and take it with me when space is limited or on an airline in checked baggage.  Everything is built into the scope so you don't need the tripod if you have a table.  Aligning the GoTo is a simple process once you have done it a few times.  The first time you do this you put in a location, time and date.  Those are retained in memory so you only do this once. Meade provides a compass/level that goes in the eyepiece hole.  You level the scope and point it North.  Then lock the two clutches so the motors can turn the scope.  Turn on the computer and select the EASY alignment option.  The scope selects a bright star that should be easily visible in your sky.  You don’t have to know where the star is, the scope knows.  Using the 26 mm eyepiece you look in the eyepiece, use the arrow keys to center it and then hit enter.  The scope selects a second star and goes to it.  Again you get it in the center of the eyepiece with the arrows on the control.  Hit enter and you are done.  So easy!  Now it can find stars, planets, Messier Objects, deep space objects and more.  The ETX 80 also has a cool Tour feature that will take you on a tour of the best objects in the sky tonight.It goes from the brightest to the dimmest.  The level of light pollution in your skies are will determine how dim of an object you can see.  If you don’t know what to look for the scope will show them to you.  In this way you start to learn some of the bright stars and some of the brighter objects in your sky.  You can change eyepieces to go up in magnification any time you like.  When I do this I often also look at the target with my binoculars to become even more familiar with the sky.  When I consider this package based on price, what I got in the package and the beautiful wide views, I consider it a very good value.  This would be a great starter scope for anyone. You don’t have to know a lot about the sky to get started and the scope will let you use it manually when you like.  The stability, light weight, compact size and ease of use would make this a great starter for a teen too.  People are using this scope for entry level photography, webcam video astrophotography and more.  There are lots of videos on YouTube.  I have since purchased an Orion XT8i Intelliscope.  This is an 8” Dobsonian scope with PushTo computer assistance which I also highly recommend.  It was always my plan to have two scopes plus binoculars.  One would be a larger scope, 8”, one a grab and go portable refractor and I will always have binoculars.  However, with all the options I have at hand the ETX 80 still gets plenty of sky time when I want to be set up fast, when I want to be able to track the target or when I want that wide view experience.  I took a 4 hour trip by car recently to a remote site.  The ETX came with me.  It is amazing how much more you can see under darker skies.  I recently went to an observing session with one of the local astronomy clubs.  I brought the ETX 80 and set it up GoTo so it would track.  I put in on the Pleiades and left it there tracking so people could see that beautiful cluster that looks much better in the ETX 80 than in my 8” Dob.  LaterI put it on the double star Albireo with the 9.7 mm eyepiece so they could see the double star split and left it tracking for half an hour.  In parallel I set up my Orion XT8i Intelliscope Dobsonian to show some of the other things in the sky while the ETX 80 tracked whatever I wanted it to track.  At some point I plan to try webcam based video photography and the ETX 80 will be my telescope of choice for this use.  Will the ETX 80 be a good scope for you?  Well if your criteria are like mine then yes.  If you think this is going to compete with an 6” $800 SCT, or a 6"  Dob then you will be disappointed.  If you are looking for high magnification then this is not the scope for you.  But if you look at it for what it is, a great entry level, wide view GoTo scope at a good price on a solid mount with lots of accessories and options available then it is a great scope and a great value. I will have this a long long time.  Even now that I have the 8" Dob the ETX continues to get its share of sky time.  Edit:  It has been a year since I purchased this scope.   I am getting deeper and deeper into astronomy. The ETX 80 continues to serve me well.   Based on its tracking ability I am now adding a video astronomy accessory and this will be the scope I use for that purpose.

review_body:
[[VIDEOID:c42f14bd068c6f0ca812c497647060b3]] ✏️ Quick thoughts to supplement my video demonstration.

Everything you need is included except for a monitor (one that accepts either HDMI or VGA) and a hard drive (just a basic laptop hard drive, \\"SATA\\" like this one: [[ASIN:B00AAKF8KC Generic 320 GB 320GB 2.5 Inch Sata Laptop Internal Hard drive 5400 RPM For Laptop/Mac/PS3 (320 GB)]].

I like this security system because:
- It's very easy to setup. Yes it takes a while (lots of steps) but it's relatively easy compared to other systems.
- There are a ton of features--everything from motion detection (which works wonderful) to an email alert system when it detects something (you have to be hooked up to a wired network of course). You can also schedule out when exactly you want it to record (e.g. after business hours).
- Easy navigation: Just need a mouse (included). Click around and right click to \\"go back\\" in the navigation.
- Very smooth, excellent quality footage. Not like that choppy stuff you see on old CCTV security systems.
- Tons of long cables. 60 foot cables (8 of them!). Note: Due to the length of the cable, there's a slight 1 second delay from the event to when you see it on your monitor.
- Full metal, tough camera design.
- Awesome in low-light/darkness. Infrared lights work wonderfully to light up the room when it's dark. (of course the human eye can't see infrared, but it lights up enough for the camera to film everything)
- Incredibly good price here on Amazon. Just factor in a hard drive and a monitor.

Overall I am very impressed with this camera system. An excellent bang for your buck, especially considering how many cameras they give you.

I was given a sample of this product in exchange for a review and demonstration. Hope demonstration and test helps!

📍 Bottom line: would I recommend this product to one of my friends?
👍 Yes, absolutely.

Overall, I'd highly recommend this bag if you want a compact, well-made bag for your 7" field monitor.

review_body: These cameras seemed great until I actually tried to mount them outside... I bought one and used it inside my window for a couple of weeks before I bought another one. It took me a lot of trial and error to finally figure out why I couldn't get the camera to upload files to Dropbox. Some settings in the current firmware (5.93) will tell you your syntax isn't right, some don't, so you're left on your own to figure it out. Customer services was quick to answer Emails but when I showed them screen shots of my settings which had improper syntax in the file names, they just told me it should work. luckily after hours of wasted time I figured it out on my own. Then I bought another one. This one went upstairs but it was dropping out. This camera was no more than 10 feet from a very high quatlity, high speed router. It finally just died! I tried everything customer service suggested. Hours upon hours were wasted doing firmware dumps and re flashes. Occasionally the camera would begin to work again, then poof! GONE again... Once I explained that I had purchased this camera from Ebay but that it was drop shipped directly to me from "Trivision LLC" They informed me that it wasn't actually their address and they would not help me further as I purchased it from an unauthorized retailer on Ebay. This Kentucky address turned out to be an Amazon/UPS shipping center and apparently some retailers carry inventories at these centers for quick shipping according to my delivery person. Apparently, even though the label said it was shipped directly from Trivision  LLC, to my home address and my full name, (I emailed a picture of this label) They would not honor an exchange or return so I had return it to the center and wait to get my money back from the drop shipper. I got my money back but my money was tied up for weeks and all I wanted was a working camera... Enter the next nightmare. I figured it was just bad luck with that camera because the first one seemed to be working fine and I already had so much time wrapped up into getting everything figured out I figured I'd give one more a shot. So it came and everything seemed fine until I put it upstairs in the same place as the last camera that failed. Same thing started happening! I figured, It has to be interference from something?! I spent days off for the next two weeks screwing with this thing until today when I wasted my entire Saturday determined to figure out what was going on. Well I finally figured it out after turning every other wifi product in my house off and countless other crazy things. These camera work great until you put them on an outside wall or in the wrong spot, the video may look good and everything will seem great but once motion is detected it seems to kill the cameras, usually temporarily, but eventually it seems that it can actually permanently destroy it as was the case with the second one I had, . I used a wifi tester and other devices had great reception in these same exact spots outside and upstairs but once I put the cameras on an outside wall of my house even as little as 4 feet from my router they would work until the motion detection triggered and then POOF! gone! stop the app wait for a few minutes and the camera would mysteriously come back. I went to the other end of my home to the camera that has been working fine and put the camera on the outside of the window glass where it has worked for weeks, SAME THING! Now I know why the guy told me I should hard wire these. I wouldn't have wasted my money on wireless cameras if I wanted to spend more time and money to make them work properly or have wires everywhere. My house is tiny. It is built of wood. I have insulated the walls myself. there is no foil backed insulation or anything of that nature that would cause interference, and my wifi signal works fine for my phone and tablet. Inside the house the cameras work great except for the window upstairs. As soon as I try to mount these cameras outside on thewall and motion is detected... They shut down for minutes at a time and I have to close anyscene or the browser and wait for them to come back. I wasted so much time figuring out what was really wrong with these it's unbelievable... I finally discovered that if I used an extension cable to get the antennas wired back through the wall on the inside of the house they will work most of the time. depending on where they are. The windows upstairs in my loft which is literally 6 feet from a really good router is nothing but trouble. and the floor is a single layer of inch and a half wood. (upstairs loft in an A frame) I tried mounting this camera on at at least 7 different locations on the same wall afraid that something must be interfering with the signal before I figured this out. With all of the time I've wasted trying to get these things to work properly, I could have bought the most expensive cameras in the world and saved money in regards to time spent... I'm really regretting this purchase right now and unfortunately it's to late to return the first camera, probably the second one as well.... I will be ordering a couple of extension cables ($3 on Ebay) to try and locate the antennas on the insides of the walls they are mounted on in positions that agree with these extremely finicky cameras, otherwise, I will unfortunately have to hard wire these to my router which I really don't want to have to do.  I'm certainly not throwing any more money than that at these. I have a feeling they won't last long anyways, especially after the one that seems to have died because of this problem. I can't say for sure, but it seems that the other camera may have killed itself trying to connect over and over. After the grief I've endured with these, I really can't recommend these cameras to anyone unless you plan on hard wiring them to your router. I'm really surprised by all of the glowing reviews here. That's why I bought them in the first place... I also notice the price has been dropping quickly recently on these too. Gee I wonder why?! And I get the feeling that all the brand new ones showing up on Ebay are the companies way of dumping them without having to be responsible for the problems or returns... Hopefully I will save someone else the trouble...

It gives the widest true field of view possible in a 1.25" barrel eyepiece, gives a generous amount of eye relief (15mm, maybe tight if you have to wear eyeglasses while observing, but very comfortable otherwise), has amazing optical quality, and isn't too heavy (about 8 ounces - solid, but shouldn't cause balance issues). The only notable optical issue is some "pincushion" distortion, which adds a little bit of curve to straight lines. This might be noticeable in daytime terrestrial use, and when panning across dense star fields, but it doesn't bother me and usually goes by completely unnoticed in my usage.

It also has a certain quality that makes you love it - it's an often cited eyepiece on astronomy forums when the topic turns to "What's your all-time favorite eyepiece". It tops my list, for sure.

product_title: Canon XA20 Professional Camcorder
review_body:
This camera does pretty much everything that I expected/hoped of it.
Since Japanese video camera vendors insist on crippling consumer cameras so as not to cannibalize their pro market, this is probably the best way to get decent functionality, high quality video, and good manual control.

Japanese camera manufacturers also consistently try to gouge their customers by asking absolutely ridiculous prices for any extras, such as a battery to replace to replace deliberately low capacity one supplied. In this case, $190 for a battery. Fortunately, there are third party alternatives which are MUCH cheaper. Why do they insist on making their customers feel ripped-off and almost regretting their purchase?

The one big disappointment in the camera itself is the quality of the electronic viewfinder (EVF).
The focus control is a small slider underneath the viewfinder, VERY difficult to set accurately, and the optical quality of the EVF lenses seems to be severely lacking, being impossible to get the rather small screen completely in focus and undistorted across the entire screen. The EVF was one of my prime reasons for buying this camera, since I find it next to impossible to use a fold-out screen in anything approaching bright sunlight.

Perhaps I was just spoiled by the XL1 viewfinder, but I find this part of the camera really disappointing.

product_title: Sigma 150-600mm F5-6.3 DG OS HSM ( C ) Lens
review_body:
I'm a beginning hobbyist so take my thoughts on this lens with that in mind. I think its a great lens and an amazing value. I've included a few images taken with the lens over my first 72 hours of ownership. Luckily, the day the lens arrived there was a full moon. I mounted the lens to a D750, threw it on a tripod and waited for a window in the clouds to get the moon shot. I have zero background in astrophotography so I'm sure it leaves a lot to be desired but that moon picture is miles better than anything I've tried in the past, even though there was a lot of smoke in the atmosphere from the forest fires a couple of states away. The photograph of the bee was taken just beyond the minimum focus distance, at 600mm, I cropped away probably 3/4 of the photo. The picture of the mountain goats is one I'd like to be able to take again; I think I had the shutter speed at 1/125 which was waaaay too slow for moving animals but it does show how well the optical stabilization works as the shot was handheld at 600mm.

The lens compares favorably to my Nikon 70-200 f4. I took a shot of a distant flower in my neighbors yard with the Sigma 150-600mm set at 200mm and the Nikion 70-200mm also at 200mm. The Sigma was just as sharp as the Nikon, my untrained eye couldn't tell the difference between the two photos. I then did a comparison at 400mm between the Sigma 150-600mm and the Nikon 70-200mm with a TC-20e III. Nikon lists their 70-200mm f4 as being compatible with the TC-20e III but with auto-focus limitations; it auto-focused fine on my D750. This is where the Sigma was the clear winner, it was much sharper. Now I'm wondering why I ever invested in the 2X teleconverter in the first place, oh I remember, because this lens wasn't available at the time!

The build quality is really good, it has a quality feel to it but I can definitely tell it's not a Nikon lens. A Nikon lens just has an excellent tactile feel to it that's hard to describe in words. Factor in the value proposition of the Sigma and the build quality exceeded my expectations.

I really appreciated the light weight. The lens mounted on a D750 (without the Tripod mount) was 6lbs 2oz total. My arms did get tired shooting with it and that's when I realized I really wouldn't want to add much more weight to my setup if I'm going to shoot handheld.

I used the Sigma USB dock (not included) to program my personal preferences which are then selected via a three position switch on the lens. It took less than 5 minutes and worked flawlessly. Having the ability to adjust preferences and update firmware via software is a very nice feature.

I only have one minor complaint, the focus ring isn't very wide at all. This might be a moot point as the auto-focus worked fast and nearly flawlessly. I only used manual focus when I took the shot of the moon.s. Factor in the value proposition of the Sigma and the build quality exceeded my expectations.

I suggest placing them at a level you can clean then off with a broom but high enough to deter vandalism.

product_title: Canon G12 10 MP Digital Camera with 5x Optical Image Stabilized Zoom and 2.8 Inch Vari-Angle LCD OLD MODEL
review_body:
I've been very happy with Canon Powershot cameras over the years -- I've had one model or another since 2003. When my trusty older model finally became outdated, I was eager to try out the G12 since it gets good review and is one the few models left with a Variangle LCD screen, which is indispensable to me for close up macro photography.

This camera has been a disappointment for several reasons:

1) The macro is very difficult to get in focus. After experimenting with Continuous AF mode and related features I've been able to get it work somewhat consistently, but nothing -- NOTHING -- like in previous, cheaper models. The higher resolution photos of the G12 compared to previous models means nothing if the camera won't focus. Manual focus is an option for macro, but the dial is very poorly designed for manual focus and consequently it isn't a practical alternative.

2) I sent the camera in to have the lens replaced after dropping the camera a couple of years ago, and Canon did that - brand new lens assembly. However, ever since I had that replaced, the telephoto has worked very poorly, having a great deal of difficulty focusing. Manual focus is also an option here, but even with focus set to infinity for far away objects, the objects (and usually whole photo) come out very blurry. In other words, there's no alternative for telephoto shots, which means I'm stuck with wide angles. Wide angles can be cropped, but it shouldn't have to come to that.

3) The camera take a verrrry long time to process a photo... that is, for the thumbnail to fade so you can see to take another photo. Very slow operation. Granted, this model is now going on five years old, but even so, unnecessarily slow by modern standards, which may cause you to miss some good shots unless you take a burst of photos... but then you can't see what your taking pictures of, since the thumbnail lingers and lingers. Not very impressive.

I really wanted to likethis camera, and would have if it had performed even as well as previous models, along with the upgrade to higher resolution. However this model has me looking at Nikon for my next camera, whether P&S or d-SLR. I'm disappointed not just in the camera, but that Canon seems to have lost its mojo with this model. review_body:
I bought this backpack in 2011 and depending what I'm shooting it carries up to 3 DSLR bodies, 4 lenses, 1 external flash, several bags of batteries, memory cards and other various accessories. I've used it for 4 years and although it gets terribly heavy because I have it packed, it is incredibly sturdy and solid and maintains its shape no matter how heavy it gets.

Yesterday I shot a party. It was outdoors and there was an outdoor bar. My back was to the bar, the bag was on the floor at my side and I was shooting the peple at the table in front of me. Behind me, someone was making a 2 gallon batch of sangria on the bar. Suddenly, a hole the size of a baseball broke out of the glass jar, and two gallons of sangria started shooting out and raining down on my bag. I grabbed it fast but it was totally saturated. I never pre-treated the fabric in any way.

Surprisingly, I unzipped it, and everything inside was dry! I quickly removed my gear and although the outside was soaked, everything inside was sangria free. When I got home, I washed the bag with laundry detergent in a washtub, spun it in the dryer and hung it open on the line overnight. Now the bag is still just as sturdy as the day I got it except now it smells like Tide, lol. It doesn't claim to be waterproof but I know that after 4 years of constant use this bag protected my gear from a major accident and it stayed firm and durable after a washing. I'm extremely thrilled and needed to share. It's A LOT of bag for 30 bucks.

product_title: GW High End CCTV Surveillance HD-SDI Security Camera, 2.1 Megapixel, 1080P Video Output Mode, Vari Focal Zoom Lens, 72 PCs IR LEDs
review_body:
This is a heavy, and bulky camera. It will allow you to set the zoom, and focus, but only manually, and only at the camera.

What I like about the camera, is the cable is routed through the mounting arm, into your wall, so nobody can easily walk up, and snip your video cable.

The mounting arm is very hefty, and rugged. It stays put when locked down.

I strongly recommend you have a portable 7, or 8 inch monitor with you when you put this camera up. You'll need someone to hold the camera for you while you use the tiny joy stick on the cable to access, and manipulate the menus to adjust the camera prior to mounting. Once mounted, you might want to make sure you can take a small monitor to wherever you put the camera up, and make whatever changes need to be made via the menus.

The camera does have digital zoom, in addition to the physical zoom.

My major gripe is that you can not turn off the LEDs. Even if you set it to be colour for day, and night, the LEDs will still snap on, and if you're shooting through a window, this is a MAJOR PROBLEM. However, you can mitigate this by putting gaffer's tape, or electrical tape over the LEDs.

If the IR mode is used instead of colour day, and night, the IR mode switches at about the right times.

You will need to buy a power supply brick, and cable. A 1Amp, 12Volt brick will do nicely. Also, don't forget to buy the appropriate length of cable, preferably one which provides power, as well as video. I tried to use an HD type cable since the camera has a green, and yellow output cable, but the HD was not detected on my HD monitor. Don't know what's up with that. Still haven't heard back from the factory regarding this. Maybe I'm using the wrong cable type. Don't know, really.

The size of this camera makes for a good visual presence on the premises, but I'd prefer a much smaller form factor.

product_title: Sony Alpha a7S Mirrorless Digital Camera
review_body:
I recently spent three weeks photographing, among other things, interiors of the great cathedrals, palaces, and castles of Spain and Portugal. I had tackled similar challenges in other countries using other good low-light cameras including the A99. What the A7S does in dimly lit interiors is, as my title says, astounding. You can be in a situation that looks gray and shadowy to the point that you can't see much detail or color with the naked eye. Then you look through the viewfinder on the A7S, and it's like somebody turned on the lights. The colors come alive, and the details pop out. Then, the actual shot typically looks even better than the viewfinder image.

At one point, my wife and I were looking at a dark interior cathedral wall that contained an elaborate array of organ pipes. I showed her how it looked on the A7S rear display. She said, "It looks like a spotlight is shining on it!"

To get these effects, I put the ISO on auto and went with shutter priority to allow good hand-held operation. In that circumstance, the camera is going to go to the largest aperture and set the exposure to look like an illuminated scene. The images I got in these circumstances had very, very little grain. As an aside, the camera's noise management (if you choose to shoot jpeg rather than RAW) is superb (and it hasn't always been that way with Sony as I relate later).

Another way I used this camera effectively was for indoor candid portraits. Using HDR, even in backlit situations, most shots came out better than if I'd used flash fill. I do occasionally use flash, but I never bothered with flash on the S. Even so, it was comforting to know that I could use a very small flash and get the same results on the S that would require a big honking flash with any other camera. That high ISO capability has the side benefit of downsizing your flash requirement. (The 4-stop advantage reduces required flash power by a factor of 16.)

In all of my shooting to date, I've yet to see noticeable noise on any shot but one. That one was made outdoors in the black of night with only a few scattered lights around. The ISO for that shot was 409,600, and even then the image was dark. Auto ISO will go that high in pitch black. In retrospect, I should have tried multi-frame noise reduction to see how much it would have helped. I'll try doing that and check back later with an update.

Another way the A7S high-ISO capability helped out was shooting from a moving platform. For example, in Seville, we took the classic horse-drawn carriage ride. The carriage was continuously jerking forward and backward. I had a zoom lens with built-in stabilization, but the oscillations of the jerking motion were too great for the stabilization to correct. No problem. Just crank the ISO way up and shoot with a super high frame rate. The images came out tack-sharp with no grain at all. Even when I was just walking outdoors, I tended to set the ISO to 800 minimum. There was just no point in shooting ISO 100 or 200 unless I wanted a long exposure with short depth of focus.

I made heavy use of in-camera HDR on this trip (which isn't available, unfortunately, in RAW). HDR pushes the exposure in dark areas by shooting multiple shots with varied exposure and superimposing higher exposure in darker areas. I'm used to seeing grain when I do this with dark scenes. Again, I saw no grain.

I confess to initially being skeptical about the A7S. In order to have smaller, lighter lenses to go with the A7 line of small, light, mirrorless bodies, Sony went with higher minimum F numbers (e.g., F4 for the 24-70 Zeiss zoom compared to F2.8 for the much bigger Alpha lens). In addition, Sony did not put optical stabilization in the new FE prime lenses, and my other Sony-Zeiss alpha lenses didn't have it either. What good was a low light sensor if I forfeited aperture and stabilization, I asked.The only reason I ended up with an A7S (and some FE lenses) was that my wife wanted to give me something for our 25th anniversary. I'm now a true believer in the A7S.

Sony has now come out with the A7R II. I'm thinking about getting it as a companion to the S. I've got the lenses, which are a big part of the expense. Even with it's backlit sensor, The A7R II can't touch the S when it comes to low light. Nothing can. What the A7R II backlit sensor does is help out a lot when you try to make individual sensor detectors very, very small. The S will benefit proportionately less because of its larger detectors. I do shoot a lot of landscapes, and I often need to crop. That's the only pressing reason for me to go to the A7R II, and even if I had it, I'd stick with the S for most shooting.

When people complain about the A7s, they often cite short battery life. Even an A99 has longer battery life (which says a lot). What we have to realize is that when we downsize everything we have to pay a price, and not just in lens aperture. An A99 battery has 150% more weight and volume than an A7s battery, yet the little A7s battery supports the same functionality. It's no surprise that A7s batteries have relatively short lives. Unfortunately, the battery size is not reflected in the battery price as much as we might hope.

Aside from short battery life (it does come with 2 batteries), I have one other criticism of the A7S design. The A7S has this ability to go to very high ISO, yet the automatic ISO doesn't seem to take advantage of it unless pushed hard. For example, I was out today shooting with a 300mm Alpha lens using the LA EA4 adapter. The program mode set my shutter speed at 320, leaving my ISO at 100. Now this would be okay if there were some form of stabilization in play, but there was not. I'm well aware of the old speed versus focal length rule, but, to me, a faster speed would make more sense here. This camera has ISO to burn, and the automatic ISO selection should, IMHO, take advantage of it. ***Update: the A7SII has corrected this with additional flexibility in auto ISO settings.***

Another complaint (but not at all from me) is the matter of "lossy" camera RAW. In my own shots, I have yet to see a recognizable artifact from whatever RAW compression is applied. I've read the critics comments on this, but I've yet to see an example image from any critic showing a recognizable compression artifact. I assure you, I can see plenty of artifacts when I use jpeg compression as well as when I apply sharpening.

On the subject of sharpening, one of the most critical limitations on sharpening is that it brings out noise. This is another distinct advantage of the A7S: noise is extremely low, which allows much more aggressive sharpening.

On the subject of jpegs, Sony has, in the past, been rightly criticized for bad application of sharpening and noise reduction. In the A850/900, the result was a serious noise problem, which drove more people to shoot RAW and do their own noise reduction and sharpening in post. I have found jpegs from the default settings in the A7s to be extraordinarily clean. No doubt this is due in part to the low-noise sensor.

Speaking of controlling ISO, the Sony manual does a particularly poor job of explaining how to use Auto ISO with control of the maximum and minimum ISO limits. Here's the sequence:
Menu > Camera 4 > ISO > Auto.
Now scroll to the right. You'll see the max and min settings appear, which you can select and adjust over the full range of ISO choices. You don't want to overlook this because this camera is so incredibly capable at high ISO, and, as I've said, the camera tends to be way too conservative in its auto ISO selections. ***Update: Again, this was fixed with additional user controllability in the II version.***

If you have Sony Alpha lenses that youwant to use with the A7s, you'll want to get the LA EA4 adapter. I have both the EA2 and EA4. The autofocus tends to hunt very badly with the EA2. The EA4 essentially turns the camera into an SLT and improves the autofocus performance. The only downside is loss of one-half stop of exposure. The A7s autofocuses beautifully with the EA4.

As far as video performance goes, I've used it, but not enough to comment. I did do an in-depth evaluation of the A99 video, which I reviewed as mediocre due primarily to moire problems. All the professional reviews have praised video performance for the A7s. They have specifically said there is no moire issue. Their praise has had only a few caveats. Perhaps the most significant complaint is rolling-shutter skew. (A complaint from non-pros is the inability to record 4K video internally.) Otherwise, the pros are saying it raises the bar for SLR video.

So should you buy an A7S or an A7R II? If I had an A7R II as well, I'd probably use it less than the A7S unless I were only going to shoot outside in the daytime. What about waiting for an A7S II? It'll probably have built in stabilization, which certainly would not hurt. It will probably also record 4K internally. But it might be correspondingly more expensive as well as slightly larger and slightly heavier with even worse battery life. ***Update: The A7SII fixes pretty much all of my complaints about the A7S. But it does cost more. Based on my own experience, if I were starting from scratch, I'd get the A7SII; but I won't sell my A7S to upgrade. [Obviously, this comment is OBE. In Apr 2016, I'm keeping the A7S, but I do have an A7RII.] I'm doing fine without the in-camera stabilization and additional ISO control, but I'd definitely pay more up front to get them.***

My bottom line is this: For me, the A7S is a magical little camera. It breaks the constraining bonds on low light, sharpening, camera shake, freezing action, and huge flash attachments. I can do so many things so much easier with it, and I can get some shots that no other camera can touch. product_title: Panasonic Video Recording Wearable Camera
review_body:
This Panasonic Ultra-Light Wearable HD action camera came well packaged and besides the camera, the box also included a multi-mount (for mounting to helmets, backpack straps, etc.), tripod mount, and IR lens. The camera is waterproof down to 5ft, dustproof, and freeze-proof to 14F. It has built-in Wi-Fi, with additional features including loop recording (which retains the most recent hour of scenes by erasing earlier scenes if recording for longer than an hour) and slow motion video.

The camera is tiny and attractive, but is of limited usage by itself due to its dependence on other devices (such as smartphones and/or tablets) for playback and to change settings. You have to download the Panasonic Image app on the devices which you will be using with this camera. I don't have a smartphone, so I downloaded the app to my iPad. At this point, I initially had a connection issue between the camera connecting to the iPad--before I went to my iPad settings and clicked on "Join Network," after which the camera immediately got connected to the iPad and I had no further issues. I don't plan to make long recordings, so this camera worked fine for me.

The nice thing about this camera is that it can also be used as a computer webcam when connecting via USB.

product_title: Thule Legend GoPro Backpack
review_body:
Seem's like all of the reviews on here are paid for, so I thought I'd write one because I bought one.

The build quality is great--very sturdy and tough material. Here is kind of a break down of the different parts:

I also made a video review: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PX7xYe70Ib4

(1) The gopro compartment: Has a nice foam casing for go pro and accessories, the top and bottom of the casing is pretty stiff, and and the side pockets are zippered and made of a tough plastic material. The gopro mount is pretty solid, it doesn't come with any mounts but i find the "vertical quick release buckle" to be the best thing to mount your gopro on here.

(2) 2 smaller pouches: Above the gopro compartment are two smaller pouches, 1 is good for bigger gopro accessories (ie. suction cup, grip mount, floaties, etc.), where the other is good for a phone/sunglasses as it's lined with a nice soft cotton material

(3) The main compartment: Pretty spacious, has 2 inner-pouches--1 for a camelbak (don't know how big; not specified) or ipad. the other is a mesh pouch, good for holding snacks or some cables maybe. Something I really wanted was a bag to hold my gopros/cameras and laptop when traveling. This bag's main compartment is big enough to hold a 15" Macbook Pro so I was pretty happy about that.

(4) Side pouches/Fanny Pack: The side pouches are fairly tall, if you put a water bottle (16 oz) it will be fully engulfed. The bag has compression belts too so if you have a monopod/selfie stick/ etc. then you can tie it down so it doesn't move. There is one on each side of the bag. The fanny pack is velcro-attached and can be removed if need be. The fanny pack has a pouch on each side good for snacks and small items (ex. keys, phone, glasses, etc.)

(5) Misc: the bag has a variety of zippers big loops and skinny stick-type ones. and a chest gopromount, which I have yet to try. In picture's and Thule's product video the bag kinda looks huge, but it's actually not that big and puffy--at least when not filled.

This bag is perfect for traveling/hiking/outdoor activities as it allows you to carry/organize your gopros and accessories while still giving you room to carry other things like a camelback laptop clothing or food. Most other bags currently on the market are only good for carrying gopros and accessories, so this bag is definitely unique.roduct video the bag kinda looks huge, but it's actually not that big and puffy--at least when not filled.

product_title: ImogenStudio QCP-A200 +Cam Pro Video Security Accessory
review_body:
PROS
For an IP (internet device), this was a relatively painless set up
Really cheap cost (compared to $200 IP cameras)
Better night vision than non infrared capable cameras
2 way sound capability

CONS
No panning
Lack of robust recording options for video

COMMENTS
I own and use some old Panasonic BR 230A cameras, which I wrote a really lengthy review to help users set them up. Compared to that camera, the ImogenStudio was easy and required only my iPhone (or your Android probably). There is no panning/tilt feature, but that appears to be where most security video IP cameras are headed (unlike my old $200 Panasonics which panned/tilted remotely). The really expensive Nest IP cameras have the highest resolution allowing the best ability without panning/zoooming options. This ImogenStudio PRO version has sufficiently wide of angle of view, however, and I did not miss the ability to pan or zoom. The picture quality is very good (compared to my old Panasonics).

With all the positives, I gave this 4 stars, because I just didn't feel that this would be a competent "security" camera because I didn't feel great about its lack of robust recording capabilities. On my old Panasonics, I had them set up to record for unbelievably long periods of time to a local desktop that was running 24/7. I had recorded maybe 4 hours of video per day with that set up, which I could review later in case I suspected something needed to be reviewed (i.e. nanny incident).

If I were to start all over, I'd look at the Drop camera, newly acquired by Nest, and wait for their newer version which should have more of the Nest design/engineering imprints on it. That camera is $200 and will probably be priced at a premium and their cloud storage is expensive, but if you want peace of mind, then you will need to spend the money.

That's no small feat, considering the legendary quality of the Summicron. I'm a professional photojournalist and reporter who travels extensively, and I can attest to the ruggedness and solid quality of the Voigtlander Nokton. The extra half-stop difference in speed is critical for indoor and low-light situations. I considered a Summilux but saved thousands by choosing the Nokton. One difference that should be noted is that the Voigtlander has a different look in the images it produces - a bit more clinical, not quite as warm, and lacking that painterly Leica glow. I still keep the Summicron in my camera bag if I want that look. Two pieces of advice: shoot this beautiful lens wide open (f/1.5) to get the maximum "pop" that separates the focused subject and the foreground/background; and go for the silver version instead of the black. It's a bit heavier (brass instead of aluminum), but much more substantial and rugged in feel. It doesn't look quite as nice on my black-bodied M9, but then again I've never been a fashion plate.

product_title: GoPro Hero4 CHDHY-401 Waterproof Digital Video Camera
review_body:
Although with hundreds of other reviews, mine will go un noticed, but I still give good reviews any ways. I bought the camera 9 months ago, struggled to understand how to get from one option to another. The very very small LCD screen in the front is not easy to read, as it tells you what mode you are in. If in the water proof case, using the back display is out of the question as it is un-useable. After using it on/off for over 5 months, I had enough, sat down and spend a few hours just playing with all the options, making changes and learning. Even being a tech person it was a trick. Now I flew through it flawlessly. Took a long trip to the BWCA and it was great! Came back home, did another function and it locked up. Did everything under the sun. It was inconsistant, but still locked up. One video I had set up died in the middle! This realy did not make me happy as it could not be done again. After a week of this I managed to find how to get ahold of GoPro support. They claim fast response, but it was not quite that fast. Several days later I get a E-mail stating they will get to me soon. About a week went by before I was contacted. I already had the case number from the first response. They had me do everything I already tried, and blamed the SD cards...... After almost 3 weeks going back and forth I was given a list of supported SD cards as they still claim they were the issue. After spending another $70 on a much slower card than I already had, the problems were worse! Needless to say, they sent me a pre-paid FedX box to sent it to them. After they got it they took 1 week to send a so called new one back to me (Aug 2015). If it were not for that, this would be a 5 Star Item. Over all proformance is good.

Results of different settings:
Time Laps - In the last update they changed how it works. You now have to major option. Time laps video or time laps pictures.
If you do the NEW video option, the camera auto makes a video for you, but if you do the picure time laps, you will get a ton of single pictures to deal with. The software it comes with will put those into a time laps video, but if you take them off of the card, you will be left with more pictures than what you want to work with. I made this mistake and was left dealing with 5,000 pictures at 12 mp each. NOT FUN. If you do use the mode that auto video, you will not be able to pull a indivigual photo out. A bit frustrating.

Video modes: Lots of size and speed options here. If you decide to shoot high speed (120 fps), you can not work with them unless you choose to use their software. I run a Mac and perfer iMovie and Motion. So you would have to create the section you shot, work it out in their software , export it and then import it into iMove. This is a lot of time consumption, but works. Their software is a lot slower on the Mac than expected. My Mac is an i7 3.5, a very fast computer and should handle it fine. iMovie handles the video without issues or speed problems. Running the camera at a higher level also seems to help the camera get hotter faster. As for the quality of the 120 fps, I was not very happy how well it frooze the frames. Maybe if I had more light it would of been better, but I had to deal with indoor school gym lights. So lower lighting has its issues. I ran this outdoors later and it shot much better. As for which size to choose, well in most cases I decided to use 720P over 1080 P as most can not see the differance for what I was doing it for. This also gave me more room on my memory cards.

Burst Mode: This is awesome. you have many options here. In most cases 30 frames in 1,2,3 or 6 seconds with a 3,5, 10 frames in 1 second. Also you can shoot 5, 7 or 12 MP. The fire hid the bullet, but the spent shell was caught in a few frames. This really made a neat picture. So the Burst mode works very well.

review_body:
As someone who is constantly losing my keys multiple times everyday, I was excited to receive the iGearPro Wireless Item Locator. I received a package containing 4 receivers in red, pink, black and orange along with a transmitter that has 4 buttons in 4 different sizes. All pieces are made with lightweight, durable ABS materials and batteries were included. I have included product pictures for reference.

The set works very well to help me find my missing keys and I can use a seperate receiver for my husband's and children's keys. The receivers were easy to pair with the transmitter. I simply turned them on one-by-one and pressed the button on the transmitter I wanted the receiver to respond to. When my keys are missing I press the corrisponding button on the transmitter and it sounds a beep until they are found. It will find my keys within a range 100ft, which is more than sufficient.

Unfortunately, this is where my excitement ends... The description stated there would be a LED torch/flashlight and neither the transmitter, nor the 4 receivers are equipped with one. The receivers do not flash. The product box pictured the transmitter as a credit card sized device that would fit into a wallet, but my transmitter is the one pictured in the product description here. The buttons slowly decrease in size and are not color coded as the description states. The product description also says that the transmitter requires 2 AAA batteries, which are not included. This is incorrect, the batteries were included and not even a single AAA would not fit the device. Honestly, I'm not sure what type of batteries are needed because the transmitter requires the removal of 3 tiny phillips screws that need an eyeglass screwdriver and the receivers each have 2 of the same screws.

All things considered, I am pleased with the quality and function of the iGearPro Wireless Item Locator and I would have been happy with the product had it fit the description on either the page, or product box. Sadly, that wasn't the case and therefore I cannot rate the Key Finder highly, even though the product is great quality and functional. I leave it on even when it isn't raining for this reason. I also use a tripod nearly 100% of the time which you need to know to make sense of this next reason. That may not seem like much, but any extra ability to cut down on visibility is a plus. Here is the third reason I like it: in the winter, the storm jacket can keep the wind off your hand, thus keeping it warm almost like a glove. There are three reasons I love the jacket — and I haven't even mentioned rain!

product_title: Celestron 94124 2-Inch UHC/LPR Filter (Black)
review_body: I use a 4" telescope in urban skies. There is nothing written about this filter other than adknowledge of it's existance by filter gurus in the amateur astronomy web comunity. Bottom line, it does a beautiful job. Otherwise invisible objects in urban skies become magically visible. Summer nebulae M8,M16,M17,and M20 get an amazing enhancement, a couple of them really amazing from nothing there to wow!. M27 and M57 are not "prettier" but i would say " more comfortable" to see. I own both a UHD and OIII lumicon filters but they are too harsh on small telescopes in urban skies. For that,I recommend this cheapo Celestron LPR. Do not be confused however!. Phil Harington lists this filter as a narrowband in his book. It is a broadband. And it works. Save your money, if you have a small telescope in poor skies this is the filter for you. Use low power. I used it from 16x to 40x to wonderful result. At 60x not so good. Happy viewing asn clear skies!

product_title: Sony SAL-70400G2 70-400mm F4-5.6 G SSM Super Telephoto Zoom Lens
review_body: It's hard to say that I believe a lens is not up to all the high praise it receives when so many people seem so happy with it, but that's my situation. I have spent a week shooting birds as well as just ordinary snaps around the garden with my new Sony 70-400 G2 on my trusty A77ii. At best I got  "shoulder shrug" results. I was expecting much better results than I get with my Tamron 150-600 USD, Tamron 70-300 USD, Minolta 100-300 APO & Minolta 100-400 APO. I'm not saying these other lenses are great; I bought  the Sony because I wanted to step up from these, but the Sony 70-400 g2 was not tack sharp even at F8. It was just OK at 400mm, perhaps a little better at 300mm. But I do large 13"x19" prints. If this was a $500 lens or even a $1000 lens, I might keep it. It's not bad. It's certainly much lighter than the Tamron 150-600. But for me to pay $2100, I have to be able to say the lens is really, really, really good, and signicantly better than any of the others I already have. It's not. It's marginally better in some cases and not at all better in others. Am I crazy? Well, DXOmark rates it as on the "poor" end of the scale for sharpness, and for birds, I need sharp! I suspect I might have bad copy, but I am not willing to fuss around with trying to get a good copy of this lens. I will return it.  Final Note: The clincher came when the clouds and rain rolled in this week. This lens HATES low light. Since the best results are not at f5.6, but at f8, that means that you must increase the ISO, which of course increases the noise. I was hoping that I could shoot wide open at the long end (I had read that it was unusually sharp for a telezoom at the long end). No chance oh getting sharp shots at the long end 99% of the time. My Sony flash helps, but not much at 400 mm ;) Disappointed.  PS: Something did seem to be not working with the AF that is probably specific to this copy of this lens.  When we first got it, I thought that the Minimum FocusingDistance had been understated. We measured the minimum distance at which I could auto focus as being 9 ft, considerably more than the stated 1.5 meters/5 ft. However, when I used Manual Focus, I could easily move closer to be subject to the 5 ft distance. I was using focus peaking to confirm manual focus. I had no problems with Manual Focus at any focal length, but I haven't perfected getting (BIF) Birds in Flight using Manual! And the shots were not superior in quality as stated above. However, the problems with AF were not consistent. Sometimes it would seem OK, then other times not OK. Most often the "Not OK" happened in low(ish) light (cloudy afternoon outside or in the house under multiple skylights without flash--I'm not talking about twilight here), while the OK AF shots were in bright daylight or with flash. My husband tried the Sony 70-400 G2 with his A6000 and the LAEA4 adapter. He had all the same issues.
