review_body:
There is nothing my review will add to all that has been posted here.
I've been using 4/3 systems since the Olympus E-5, and migrated to M4/3 with the EP-1.
I also have a GX7, which has it's use... but for the most part I've been going out with the GM5.
Is so light and confortable to carry, has all the functions, features and capabilities of other M4/3 bodies with 2 drawbacks.
One is the electronic/physical shutter, which might be an issue on specific conditions.
For most instances, not an issue for me, When using my GX7 I usually have it with electronic shutter to avoid distracting my photo victims enabling for un-staged captures.
The other is the lack of physical buttons, however I have to say, the screen is so responsive, that honestly is not such a big deal.
The EVF is there... but realistically... is just a tool in the event of strong sun light.
And battery... just buy an extra one, and shut the camera off while not in use, it will take no more than one second for it to power up and be ready for use.
Finally, to take real advantage of the size and weight, it needs to be paired with the "smaller" lenses, the "biggest" one I use on this system are the Lumix/Panasonic 25mm 1.4 and the Panasonic macro 45mm 2.8.

product_title: Fujifilm XF 27mm F2.8 Compact Prime Lens
review_body:
I've wanted this lens for a long time, but just wasn't sure about it because I already have the 35mm [[ASIN:B006UL00R6 Fujinon XF 35mm F1.4 R]]. Would this really be worth it? I kept looking for one of Fuji's semi-annual sales and when it dropped to $250 last week, I took the plunge.

Very very glad that I did. First, no, it doesn't lie near-flat on the camera as I'd hoped for but for $250 this is a nice alternative, The XF27 makes it a very light, very inconspicuous, snapshot-looking camera, taking much better photos than people actually expect..

The XF35 is a great lens, too. Beautiful quality to the photos, wonderful in low light, beautiful bokeh. But the XF27 really -does- feel like a different lens and makes the camera feel different. It is sharp and light and because you can boost the ISO so high with Fuji, even low light shots at f2.8 often are turning out, though of course the 35mm is better. The glass itself is a little over 1/2" in diameter, so when you're taking someone's photo it really doesn't look like you're taking "A Serious Picture". Perfect for street photography.

I was very surprised that the 27mm (41mm equivalent) field of view really -does- make a big difference to me compared with the 35mm. I like the 35mm--and it is lovely for portraits--but I have to admit that it is often a pretty tight shot in some places where you can't back up. The 27mm felt like a much more comfortable, more natural framing (supposedly the closest to what our eye sees)--I really did notice a significant difference--and it gives more context for people when you -want- to see the background. Again, nice for street photography.

The lens cap is tiny, with pinch edges, and I use a tether. It takes 39mm filters which are generally pretty expensive. But I got this one from Fotasy [[ASIN:B00EN0Y8S8 Fotasy MRC 39mm Pro 1-D Multi-Resistant Coating Super Slim MC UV HD Filter]]for under $10 and it's working well I put a comparison up to show the different FOV between the 35 and 27 (both at f5.6 for comparison). Really glad to have this, perfect addition to any kit I think (at the sale price).

product_title: ANART® Wifi Mini HD 1080P 2.0inch Big Screen 170 degree Wide Angle Waterproof Sport Camera+ the Medium Shockproof Carrying Bag
review_body:
[[VIDEOID:4697974f989df712b8fc937f589c3ddf]]The camera has excellent optics, and the 170º wide-angle lens has enough depth of field to capture everything from a few inches from the lens to infinity. The camera kit includes a nice starter set of GoPro-compatible mounts and accessories, an AC adapter (5V/1A), and a carrying case. In addition to the fine optics and a range of features, what really sets the camera apart from most other action cams is the ability to control the camera using an app on an Android or iOS phone or tablet, and getting a live video feed displayed on my phone.

Setting up the camera and getting it to work was pretty simple, thanks to a well written user guide (I do wish the user guide went into more detail about using time lapse and continuous time lapse). I inserted a 16GB micro-SD card, then charged the battery, and the camera was ready to go. Except for setting the date and time, I left most of the default settings as-is for the time being. The camera has two HD video modes, with files saved in MOV format:
* 1920x1080 (30 frames per second)
* 1280x720 (60 frames per second)

For still photography, the camera offers a choice of four image sizes, with files saved in JPG format in the sRGB color space:
* 12 MP (4000x3000)
* 8 MP (3264x2448)
* 5 MP (2560x1920)
* 2 MP (1920x1080)

The image quality and audio are quite good. (The audio is also good, considering that the camera is usually sealed inside the waterproof case while you're using it.) You get a wide-angle image with good auto-exposure and good color and contrast. I used the camera indoors and outdoors and got good exposures even indoors with subdued lighting.

The camera uses a replaceable 3.7-volt 900mAh Li-ion battery that can be recharged while it's in the camera using the included AC adapter. I don't know if ANART sells extra batteries, but I've ordered compatible batteries at this link: [[ASIN:B00Q5QKC8I Wasabi Power Battery (2-Pack) and Charger]].

What really sets the camera apart from most of the other action cams that I've seen is the ability to control the camera using an app on an Android or iOS phone or tablet (unfortunately, there's no app for Amazon devices). I installed the \\"iSmart DV\\" app on my Android phone. It not only allowed me to control the camera, it sent a live feed of what the camera was seeing to my phone. To use the app, first install it on your phone or tablet. Now turn on the camera and push the Wi-Fi button on the side of the camera. On your phone or tablet, go to your settings and connect with a wi-fi network named \\"ActionCam W9\\" - that's the ANART camera. Now run the app and you should almost immediately see the live feed on your phone or tablet.

If you've used an action cam before, you know how important accessories are. Basically you can't do much of anything without the mounting accessories. The camera includes a basic starter set of these accessories. As you get into using the camera, you'll likely want to buy some other accessories, such as a head mount and a chest mount, plus some miscellaneous connecting pieces. The good news is that they're not very expensive, with a lot of sellers offering them.

Could the camera be used as a dashboard camera? Well, yes, but for that purpose, I recommend a dedicated dash cam that is designed to be used in a vehicle, and has features tailored for that.

What really excites me about this camera are the endless possibilities for video and still photography, plus time lapse photography, much of which would be virtually impossible without a little action camera like this. Never having used a GoPro, I can't compare the ANART camera with a GoPro, but on its own merits, I have to say this is a fun little camera to use, with very good image quality.

The ANART wifi action cam was provided to me for evaluation. I did not promise to post a review, but I stated thatif I did review the product, it would be an honest, unbiased review.

product_title: Foscam V2 Megapixel HD 1280 x 720p H.264 Wireless/Wired Pan/Tilt IP Camera with IR-Cut Filter
review_body:
There are a few fairly significant issues with this IP Camera. The first being a browser extension which is not compatible with Chrome. Given Chrome is at least 25% of the desktop browser share, one and four of you will have issues even using this camera.

The large issue is substantial lack of proper security:
1) The max password length is 12 characters. Sure, this is 94 to the 12th in possible combinations, but there really is no technical reason to have such a limit.
2) They have pre-seeded every camera with the same exact wildcard SSL certificate to try and make the DDNS stuff not throw SSL warnings. However, in doing so they have made the device inherently insecure -- forget short passwords, should someone root this device and rip out the SSL key, a bad actor can do a man-in-the-middle with the *valid certificate* to capture your password without any hint of being compromised to view any camera you have exposed to the internet. This in itself is a serious security flaw, because there does not appear to be a way for an end user actually replace the SSL cert & key.
3) WiFi is not very strong. My camera is ~40-50" away between two interior walls, yet I barely can connect to the camera at times. My cell phone has better wifi signal strength in the same position than this camera, and the camera has an external antenna.

Despite all the bad stuff... for the price it's an *okay* camera. I just wish they would take the security of a potential security device much more seriously.

product_title: 2 batteries
review_body:
I recently purchased a Sony HX50V camera. This was my first exploration away from those inexpensive cameras with digital zoom. This Sony has a real optical lens and takes great pictures. But it came with one battery and no charger. I have to charge it by connecting it to my computer with a USB cable or using a USB wall charger that came with my smartphone and connect that to the camera with a USB cable. While it is charging, I cannot use my camera since the battery has to stay in the camera while charging.

Then, I was offered the opportunity to receive a charger and battery that was compatible with my HX50V camera in return for an honest review. When I looked at the specs for this package, there is a long list of Sony cameras this combo is compatible with. My HX50V camera was included in the list, so I thought it would be great to have this with my camera.

When the package arrived, I compared the battery in the package with my Sony camera battery - Exactly the same size and configuration. Same specs printed on the battery. Looks exactly the same with just a different label. I have supplied a picture of the batteries side-by-side. You can see they look pretty much the same.

The charger itself is pretty basic. It weighs practically nothing and made from thin plastic. Not sure how well it will hold up if it gets banged around a lot. But the battery fits securely in the slot in the charger and it does the job charging the battery. The charger has an LED light next to the OAproda brand name on the charger case that shows red while the battery is charging. The light changes color when the battery is charged.

product_title: Sony HD Video Recording HDRCX440 Handycam Camcorder
review_body:
This is a very compact camcorder that is very easy to use. It also takes pretty good video.

It's excellent in natural light and even brightly lit indoors shots; it's even pretty good in low light ... if you remember to turn on the low light setting. If you leave everything on auto, it's going to have a hard time with low light situations. What I assume that does is let it boost up the ISO, depending on the lighting situation. It goes without saying that means you're going to get a bit more grain, but that's just physics. You'd need a faster lens and a bigger chip to avoid that.

It's very easy to charge. You don't even need to carry a cable. The charger is built in, and a little USB plug inserts into the back of the handle where you don't even notice it until you are ready to charge and can pull it out. The cord on the charging plug is only a couple of inches long, so while you could plug it in directly to a laptop or a charging plug, you might need an extension. Luckily, they include a USB extender that you can plug it into and then plug that into your charger or computer.

It turns on when you open the screen. To open the lens cap you have to slide a little button near the front. When it turns on, the LCD screen shows what you'd get if you started shooting. It also shows a little menu button up in the corner. It's got all the expected functions on a camcorder, and they're easy to access via a little joystick. If you press the joystick button it opens the menu and you can go through the entire list of features. But, and I like this, you can also access the most crucial features if you press down on the joystick without going into the menu, and then your selected options will appear around the edge of the screen and you can toggle through them to change those options directly.

It has built in memory, so you can record videos directly out of the box, but you'll probably want to get a microSD card if you expect to record more than an hour or so at top quality. You can record as AVCHD files which are better quality, or as MP4 files which would be easier to view and upload. With AVCHD files you'd need to edit and convert them to another format before uploading or sharing them. I always edit my videos, so I always record in the highest quality available.

You can share the videos to a laptop or phone via wifi. I don't think I'll ever use that since I generally just record to a microSD card and then back everything up to a computer, but it's an option in case you don't have a laptop and want to upload things to your phone so you can share them.

A feature I do really like is that you can download Sony's "PlayMemories" app (on either the app store or one of the android stores) on your phone and then you can control the camera and view what it's "seeing" directly from your phone. That way you could place the camera on a tripod, sit somewhere else and still control it. You can even control the zoom remotely.

All in all this is a nice starter level HD camcorder, that records pretty good video and is very compact. It'll fit in a purse or a pocket if you like. It's not a high end or professional camcorder, but it would be a great compact camcorder to take on a trip or to have ready for all those cute things your kids or you cats do. review_body: I have several Manfrotto tripods, but I had this for almost a month now.  I happened to find it, believe it or not, @ the Salvation Army Thrift Store here in our local area.  I bought this tripod for $9.99 with a Manfrotto 234RC head, brand new, still in the plastic wrap and box.  I like the portability and weight of this tripod, but not as light as the Slik carbon fiber tripod that I already own, however it is built tougher, since it is aluminum.  The legs can be opened lower and wider with  a twist of a lever switch, just below the head base, which gives you other shooting position.  This tripod also, has a hard foam insulation on two of the three legs, situated on the upper legs, just below the head base.  The third leg is left open for the Manfrotto logo and model and serial number engraved nicely on the metal.  Because of its size, I use this tripod for my mirrorless Fujifilm XT1 cameras, which I continue to love every passing of the days that I have owned them.  I have used this tripod also with my Nikon D810 and D700 with no major issues, as long as lenses longer than 70-200mm f2.8 are not used.  Overall, this tripod is perfect along with a good head, i.e. ballhead, for smaller mirrorless cameras.

product_title: Olympus Air Mirrorless Camera
review_body:
I ordered this item a few hours after "discovering" it and reading some quick reviews. I'm probably the type of customer this is pointed towards: an existing Micro Four Thirds user with a couple camera bodies and stable of lenses, a smart phone user and a bit of a gadget hound.

It's a very interesting product and is well made and solid. Picture quality is excellent as one might expect; it has a modern four thirds sensor and current TruePic VII engine. And you can use any Micro Four Thirds lens you have on hand. It sounds great. So why did I return it?

My main issue comes down to actually handling the product. You may not have a camera body to lug around but you still need at least one lens, the Air itself and your smart phone. (Unless of course you're shooting blind and just whack the expose button on the Air and cross your fingers). It was too unwieldy for me. In fact, once the iPhone is in place in the holder the simple act of aiming, focusing and hitting the expose button is a bit of a chore. And if you're using a non-stabilized lens (every Olympus lens) you'd better be sure you don't jitter or shake whilst performing this two handed task. If you plan to use this on a tripod or simply set it down and control remotely then this is not a concern. However, I was hoping for something portable and ready to shoot.

As you may have read in other reviews there are also access issues for USB charging and the memory card. The back of the device actually has two plastic parts that must be removed to simply insert/remove the MicroSD card. The phone holder must first come off and then a second plastic covering plate. Since you can upload files from the Air via the iPhone app, or transfer via cable you may not need to access the memory card too often but it's still an odd design choice. And as mentioned, the USB port cannot be accessed unless the phone holder part is removed.

Frankly I'm still impressed with the technology on display here and would have kept the Air if I felt I would get some use out of it other than sitting around and tinkering with it. But the ungainly handling issues convinced me pretty quickly that it would spend most of its' time on my shelf. A bit disappointed. Perhaps I just had unrealistic expectations of how it would work.display here and would have kept the Air if I felt I would get some use out of it other than sitting around and tinkering with it. product_title: Neewer 24"/60cm Handheld Stabilizer with Quick Release Plate 1/4" and 3/8" Screw for DSLR and Video Cameras up to 6lbs/2.7kg
review_body: This stabilizer takes quite a bit of adjusting to get it right and then some practice to learn how to use it. It's not as good as the $300-$400 stablizers, but it's only $80. It's fairly easy to adjust the balance front to back, but very difficult to adjust side to side (see tip below). Also, try to watch some videos on-line about how to adjust the center of gravity and how to actually control the stabilizer when in use.  A few tips:  1. Get a light stand...the stabilizer has a hollow handle that will set down over the top of the light stand (see photo). This helps immensely while balancing the rig and when you want to set it down for a while. Using the stabilizer is very tiring on your arm.  2. To make the side-to-side adjustment easier, I added the Neewer Two-way 4"/10cm Macro Shot Focusing Rail Slider (see photo) to the top of the stabilizer before mounting the camera. Here's the link: http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00HLCXPMU?psc=1&redirect=true&ref_=oh_aui_detailpage_o01_s00  3. Use the widest lens, or the widest setting on your zoom lens. This will result in smoother motion.  4. Before balancing, make sure your camera is configured EXACTLY the way you will use it when shooting...i.e., the battery, SD card, filters, mics, etc. must be in place before balancing. Also, changing the setting of the zoom lens will also throw off the balance.

product_title: Yuneec Q500+ Typhoon Quadcopter with Aluminum Case, Free 32 GB Micro SD Card and Handheld CGO SteadyGrip Gimbal. Extra Battery and Extra Propellers Included.
review_body:
The Typhoon Yuneec Q500+ has a superior camera/video. It comes with its own FPV screen, an extra battery, a handheld steady grip for the CGO+ camera, and an aluminum case. The whole package only cost me only $1249.00. Delivery was very prompt (less than a week).

The Typhoon is an extremely stable aerial photography platform, thanks to a dual GPS-GLONASS positioning system. Even when it is much bigger than the other competitor quadcopters, it has a well engineered and aerodynamic design. Wind gusts will flow gracefully around the quadcopter body. The CGO+ 3 Axis Gimbal camera is very light and shaped as a ball. Thus the whole quadcopter feels very light, even when it is awkward to handle because of its size.

The quadcopter will bind with the STO+ transmitter very fast. For the competitor quadcopters, it will require more time to set up WiFi and binding before you can send the quadcopter in the air. Also the STO+ transmitter is the only one in the market with its own GPS-GLONASS system, allowing the quadcopter to return to where the transmitter is located, rather where it takes off.

review_body:
This review is for the DJI Phantom 3 Standard.

There is a lot of info on the net about the Advanced and Pro versions, not a lot about the Standard. The first thing I had to do when it was powered up was a firmware update, which went smoothly. Afterwards the copter wouldnt start, said i had to do a IMU calibration. So I searched the net, found some info about plugging the copter into your device with a USB to do the calibration. Took me 3 days to get a Micro to Micro USB, only to find out the Phantom 3 standard doesnt need the USB, it does it wirelessly.

Once that was done I went and flew it several times, very easy to fly, stable, love it. After the third flight I lost the camera view. Back to the net looking for info. Several videos and forums suggested I had to "rebind" the camera. Again, these are from other versions of the copter. The best suggestion I found was "shut off and restart your cell phone" I did that and now everything is back to normal. It takes great pictures and video.

I would say my only complaint is lack of information both from DJI and online about this new model.

The majority of people could not say enough good things about this lens and there were always a few picky people who had to find something negative but those people tend to ignore the design and quality of their purchase. It's a beautiful lens that is very sharp, fast focusing, very quiet, and locks in two positions so the telephoto barrel doesn't drift. I went out first and practiced to get a feel for the lens and review my photos before taking a trip to a national park where I was able to get some very nice shots and have some good fun. product_title: Dropcam Pro Wi-Fi Wireless Video Monitoring Security Camera
review_body: I purchased a Dropcam a little over a year ago and subscribed to the seven day recorded history plan which allowed me to watch both live and past events from the Dropcam app on my iPad.  I was slso sent emails when motion was detected.  Although the sensitivity of the motion detector often caused emails of waving tree branches, it also detected suspicious persons entering my property.   This was an important feature, as I was away from home frequently and the notifications and ability to scroll through the recorded history kept me current on what was happening at my home.  However, in the past several weeks, apparently in an attempt to force Dropcam app users to migrate to the Nest mobile app, Nest has eliminated virtuually all of the features that made the Dropcam app so user friendly.  In addition, the Nest app has now both ceased to recognize most of the motion that occurs and also to send notifications of those very few motions that it does recognize.  Apparently, Nest believes that it can learn your activities so that notifications are not necessary if it is a "recognized" activity.  However, this means that since Nest "recognizes" me walking up to my front door, it assumes that I am everyone who walks up to the door -- homeowner, solicitor, burglar -- same person.  The value of my camera for security purposes is substantially eliminated.  Because of the degrading of the Dropcam app and the extremely poor design of the Nest app as it relates to camera function, I cannot recommend purchasing a Dropcam/Nest camera.

product_title: Nikon COOLPIX S9700
review_body:
Photography is about composition, instinct, technique, and taste. The S9700 makes for an ideal set of training wheels for the aspiring photographer. This camera is lightweight, easy to use, and has a great price point. It performs well enough at moderate zoom and in plentiful light.

I emphasize ease of use because the main advantage of this camera is spending a relatively small amount of money to learn the science and the craft of photography. The pop-up flash feels flimsy but using flash should be avoided anyway. Mostly the camera is pretty durable; I've taken it under a waterfall and to the beach. It's handled small amounts of water and sand with aplomb. The LCD screen developed a small crack but frankly, I've been abusing it purposefully.

So basically, the point of this camera is to get out there and learn how to take good pictures, to learn how to frame, to compose, to learn what's attractive. It doesn't have a strong aperture range, the shutter speeds aren't fantastic, and forget about photographing in low light. Use minimum ISO or not at all. It's a camera that fits in your pocket, what do you really expect out of it?

Once you've mastered the compositional basics of photography, then I'd start thinking about a DSLR camera and all the complexities that come with it. Interchanging lenses and stuff like that. Before you've learned that, try the S9700.

review_body:
The selfie stick screwed into a compact camera works really well. The stick in combination with the phone holder is only just ok, you'll either need to use the camera timer, or get a separate bluetooth remote, and the grip is also questionable and not good with phones thicker than 8mm. It also has a problem with rotating when the stick isnt fully extended. The stick can't be used on top of the tripod, it just falls over. The tripod with the phone holder is very light weight and will blow over in the wind but it's fine inside. Overall the package is ok, but quite limited due to design flaws.

SELFIE STICK 3/5
The build quality is good, the handle is rubber, and extremely grippy. The bottom tripod mounting hole, telescopic pole, and tripod screw at the top are all metal which is good. The head where you attach the phone holder is plastic but it seems to be strong after giving it a lot of vigorous shakes. The screw to tighten it is also metal but I found it loosened a little. It works good with compact cameras, and ok with gopros.

The problem with the selfie stick is that if you shake it the camera starts to tilt/rotate sideways, especially if it's not fully extended. There are no grooves in the metal pole to stop it from rotating sideways. Also, there is no bluetooth or any kind of connection, so you will need a bluetooth remote trigger or use the self timer on the camera.
It measures 8.5" closed, and 42" fully extended.

MINI TRIPOD 2/5
The mini tripod is made almost entirely of plastic, even the ball head and tripod screw... It kind of grinds when you adjust it, and the screw already partially striped when trying to screw into the bottom of the selfie stick, it just keeps rotating in the hole, but it screws into cameras and the phone holder fine. It's ok if you want something ultra light for a compact cameras, or phones with the phone holder, but it's not sturdy enough to stay standing on a windy day, and the thin aluminium legs dont stay extended after repositioning it a few times. I have a model that looks exactly like it that's made entirely out of metal and it worked really good, but this plastic one is subpar.

PHONE HOLDER 3/5
The phone holder is made out of plastic and metal. It's spring loaded and will hold phones and thin compact cameras ranging from 55-75mm wide, and up to 8mm thick (thicker will be less secure). With my galaxy S4, it fits nicely in the indent, but if it's not fully pushed in, it slips out with a few shakes. It's also less secure with my phone case on and giving it a few vigorous shakes causes it to pop out. It's only good if it's not shaken, and should be checked between uses. The top grip should be wider and grippier rubber, and the bottom grip should be angled rubber instead of flat foam. It's good on a tripod, but I dont trust it on the stick.

review_body:

I'm no professional graphic designer, but I take pictures regularly, and has always had the doubt that however the color look on my screen, it will look different on another viewer.

After calibrated with spyder 5 express, which only takes 5 mins on me, and maybe 15 mins in total, the color cast is all gone. There is still a very slight color difference (hue, saturation) between 3 screens, but I attribute that to the display quality itself. Now the white color looks the same. It might still looks different on someone else' screen, but if theirs get calibrated as well (which I believe all professionals, and most prosumers do), the difference should be minimum.

One thing to notice is how the software interact with windows 10. Initially I switched to my laptop monitor view only, calibrated it, then switched to monitor display only, calibrated it, then I switched to the extended mode. Windows 10 only use the color profile for the monitor display, and therefore, the color on the laptop display was still off. So I calibrated the monitor display again, but in the extended mode. Now they are the same. I suspected that there is some configuration in windows that would allow you apply color profile to each display directly, but I didn't spend the time figuring it out. The calibration process was fast enough that I just did it again.

Overall, I'm very happy with the product, and will recommend this to other people.

review_body: EDIT December 2, 2015 - Although this camera has an IR filter that flips in and out of place, it frequently gets stuck in the night position resulting in washed out colors during the day.  Once it gets stuck it never gets unstuck.  You can actually see this in the pictures I attached with the original review.  For my purposes, this isn't a drawback so my review remains 5 stars.  Overall, this is a great camera.  It will primarily be used as a baby monitor and has a surprisingly good microphone on it.  I was able to clearly hear the clink of dishes being put away ~35 feet from the camera as well as the bass rumble of trucks driving down the road outside our house.  The picture quality is very good also.  When I bought the camera it was the same price as the model without the built-in H.264 encoder, so I got it to try out even though I'll be using it with a Pi 2 (which has a H.264 encoder).  PROS: - great microphone, even with the base pressed firmly against a wall - very bright IR LEDs that go a good distance if needed - wall mounting hardware was included - the camera easily rotates in the base, even to a 90 degree angle inside the base with the camera pointed through the U shaped groove you see in the product image - the base itself can rotate which will be nice after it is mounted to the wall  - not about the camera directly, but the seller was great to work with as this camera was listed as a product in response to a question I sent them  SO-SOs or DONT CAREs: - cable is black; I'm not sure if I'm going to try to wrap it in white tape or something or leave it as the cable is the maximum length allowed by USB (5 meters) - as just mentioned, this camera has a very long USB cable which doesn't matter for me but could be useful for someone else - the camera's orientation doesn't match the little arrow on the case but is easy to figure out - the groove that the USB cable fits through on the base could be a little deeper  CONS: - H.264 encoding wasn't the best and alsowas a much higher bitrate than the Pi encoder produced (720p: Pi ~300Kb/s, ELP ~4Mb/s).  This isn't really an issue for me as I was planning on using the Pi in any case as it allows me to modify the raw YUV easily and do things like add a timestamp to the display.  It's also possible that I didn't have V4L2 or gstreamer set up properly.  The attached pictures are of our crib at nighttime with the door closed in full darkness and the next with the light on.  Overall, a great camera and I'll likely be buying more cameras from this seller in the future.

[[VIDEOID:e7cf3e6f38f621152b32f13db3dae041]] What an incredible sports camera. This little jewel is quite small, but still records at 1080p with exceptionally high quality. You can even set up the camera and start it using the wifi app. Since I'm just getting started using this little beauty, I'm still discovering one neat feature after another that I didn't expect in such an inexpensive package. review_body: I see many negative reviews of this camera but I have to say that I have had 4 of these for more than 2 years now and no problems. I have them working with IE 11 Windows 7 64 Bit, IE 11 Windows 10 64 bit, and IE 8 XP 32 bit without any issues. You do need to have some tech knowledge of how to setup IPs and Port Forwarding via your router and firewalls. Once you do that and install the Swann ActiveX Control on your client PCs, it works flawlessly. These are not High Def and I would not recommend high def unless you have a lot of upload bandwidth. My upload bandwidth is 6 GB with a cable modem. Upload speed is the important number here, not download speed. High def can require much more bandwidth and limit the number of cameras you can support. With that said, Swann Tech support were absolutely no help for me when I was trying to get mine installed. After a few web searches and downloading the updated SwannActiveX.exe Control install file, I was off and running.

review_body:
The Neewer LED lights have become an essential part of my camera kit for all my nightclub photography gigs. The dimmable switch allows you to finely adjust your light output to fit the environment and capture great quality video, even in the darkest of club locations.

The housing for the lights is made from a thinner plastic, which decreases its ability to take a hard bump, but in no way makes it feel fragile. The positive tradeoff is that it makes the entire unit very lightweight. This is very important feature, as walking around for hours on end during a shoot with a heavier system attached to my camera would most likely get quite tiresome.

The lights easily attach to the hotshoe on all my cameras, and works well with Sony's Li-ion rechargeable batteries. I highly recommend this product to all videographers who are looking into purchasing a lightweight, portable lighting system.

product_title: Celestron 93235 CrossAim Reticle Eyepiece (Black/Silver)
review_body: Received this recently for a first try out last evening.  The goals were dual purpose: 1) to aid with star alignment so that my goto system can be accurate and for the best polar alignment routine and 2) as a guiding eyepiece when using an off axis guider.  I use a refractor and my camera does not tether live view functions to my laptop, so I am using a flip diagonal along with this eyepiece to do alignments on stars.  The eyepiece arrived in a timely manner with adequate packing, but it immediately failed to light up!  I changed out the batteries and still nothing.  Being in a pinch for a real *need* to have the eyepiece asap, I decided to mount my own AAA set in holder and then used velcro to attach to the eyepiece (and also bypassing the on/off switch and dimmer adjustment) .  This worked, but shouldn't have had to be done considering the cost of the eyepiece.  Another thing I found is that the eyepiece would not quite reach focus.  I get close enough, but with my combination, the eyepiece or eyepiece tube need to be about 1/4" shorter and then it would focus.  Not sure why this is; when I swapped out the eyepiece for a 40mm wide field one I had, I was easily able to reach focus.  Again, for the cost, this should be.  Basically, if your in a hurry as I was, and know how to bypass the electronics for your own if they are DOA, and don't mind putting up with slight misfocus, then this eyepiece would do.... otherwise I would avoid or make your own from a spare eyepiece.

product_title: Polaroid Z2300 10MP Digital Instant Print Camera
review_body:
This camera is fun for the price point.

I have only had the camera a few weeks. Since there have been quite a few reviews already posted, here are just a few thoughts based on my experience to date.

CAMERA BUILD: It feels like an inexpensive camera, perhaps because it is one. It has been described as bulky. My response would be 'Compared to which other cameras that print pictures?" I am impressed at its size versus what it can do. I concur with input from other buyers that the door to the printer paper pops open too easily. Likewise, I find the camera sometimes turns on when I am just putting it in the case. I find these minor annoyances.

EXTRA BATTERY: I got an extra battery. Contrary to what was written in a prior review, I have not had to reset the date & time when swapping batteries at an unhurried pace. I am not challenging the prior review, but rather speculating that there is a limited window of time in which the swap can be done without loosing that date/time data.

POLAROID CASE: A complete waste of money. I subsequently ordered a Case Logic CPL102. Camera plus two packs of paper and spare battery all fit in it. It comes with both a belt loop and over-the-shoulder strap.

PRINTS: I have taken about 75-100 pictures so far and printed out about 15. In keeping with every Polaroid camera that I have ever had, the picture is more about instant gratification than image quality. That said, I have found the image quality quite good. The picture is certainly not what I can do using a high-end printer for an image pulled from the SD chip and run through Lightroom, but it is respectable. The biggest problem I have with the prints is that they are a mite small. To make them look bigger, I have cut up some stiff paper into 4.25" x 3" pieces on which (using Excel) I had faintly printed a centered rectangle just under 3"x2". I peal off the adhesive back off a Zink print, mount iton the paper using the faint lines to position it and presto, it is a framed picture that look larger.

PRINTING PICTURES TAKEN ON OTHER CAMERAS: Let me preface the following by saying that I have only tried this with one camera - a Canon S120 shooting hi-res RAW in3:2 format. I took the 32GB chip out of that camera and put it in the Polaroid. I could see the pictures taken with the Canon. I tried to print one. It worked. Again, this was a highly limited experiment from which I am not prepared to make any generalized statement about the ability in print pictures taken by other cameras.

review_body:
- CHEST MOUNT 5/5
The chest mount is plastic and fabric. The plastic is really thick and doesnt seem like it will break under vigorous use. The camera stays in place during lot's of motion. The straps are a stretchy fabric material and measures 1.5 inches wide. The straps are adjustable on the sides, back, and shoulders, and should fit on chests with a diameter of 24" to 65". - HEAD STRAP 5/5
The head strap is thick plastic, and the straps are 1.5 inches wide and stretchy. On the inside is a line of rubber coating that helps with grip. The strap should fit a head diameter of 10.5" and larger. Same quality as the chest mount.

- J-HOOK + TRIPOD MOUNT ADAPTER + SCREW 5/5
They seem comparable to official gorpro pieces, maybe slightly cheaper but still strong. The tripod mount adapter has a metal screw hole. The only issue is sometime when screwing, the screw doesnt feel liek it will screw in, so I have to

- SELFIE STICK 3/5
The build quality is good, the handle is rubber, and extremely grippy. The bottom tripod mounting hole, telescopic pole, and tripod screw at the top are all metal which is good. The head where you attach the phone holder is plastic but it seems to be strong after giving it a lot of vigorous shakes. The screw to tighten it is also metal but I found it loosened a little. It works good with compact cameras, and ok with gopros, but it's not strong enough to be trusted with extreme sports use.

When positioned correctly, it's fine with gopros, but the problem with the selfie stick is that if you shake it the camera starts to tilt/rotate sideways, especially if it's not fully extended. There are no grooves in the metal pole to stop it from rotating sideways. Also, there is no bluetooth or any kind of connection, so you will need a bluetooth remote trigger or use the self timer on the camera.
It measures 8.5" closed, and 42" fully extended.

- MINI TRIPOD 2/5
The mini tripod is made almost entirely of plastic, even the ball head and tripod screw... It kind of grinds when you adjust it, and the screw already partially striped when trying to screw into the bottom of the selfie stick, it just keeps rotating in the hole, but it screws into cameras and the phone holder fine. It's ok if you want something ultra light for a compact cameras, or phones with the phone holder, but it's not sturdy enough to stay standing on a windy day, and the thin aluminium legs dont stay extended after repositioning it a few times. I have a model that looks exactly like it that's made entirely out of metal and it worked really good, but this plastic one is subpar.

- PHONE HOLDER 3/5

With my galaxy S4, it fits nicely in the indent, but if it's not fully pushed in, it slips out with a few shakes. It's also less secure with my phone case on and giving it a few vigorous shakes causes it to pop out. It's only good if it's not shaken, and should be checked between uses. The top grip should be wider and grippier rubber, and the bottom grip should be angled rubber instead of flat foam. It's good on a tripod, but I dont trust it on moving stick.

The strap, buckles, screws, and mounts are all high quality. The fabric material is thick and stretchy, with lots of room for adjustment.
The selfie stick screwed into a compact camera works really well, and it works ok with gopro when positioned right. The stick in combination with the phone holder is only just ok, you'll either need to use the camera timer, or get a separate bluetooth remote, and the grip is also questionable and not good with phones thicker than 8mm. It also has a problem with rotating when the stick isnt fully extended. The stick can't be used on top of the tripod, it just falls over. The tripod with the phone holder is very light weight and will blow over in the wind but it's fine inside.

product_title: Ion 1011L Air Pro Lite Wi-Fi Camera
review_body:
For what I paid (I got this thing dirt cheap), I'm happy with what I got:
- Really good graphic quality
- Very easy operation
- Easy to carry around

It does have its issues though:
- Setup can be a pain. If you want your videos and pictures to have the correct date/time stamp, you need to connect your camera to a computer and run a setup utility.
- It needs semi-frequent resets...on days when I really have my heart set on recording sometimes I'll flip the camera on and get that never-ending vibration that tells you you need to find a paperclip and reset the thing
- It needs frequent recharging...case in point, sometimes I like to video my bike commute to work, which is about 45 minutes. On the return trip if I don't recharge, I get maybe two, three minutes of juice.
- This is advertised as a helmet cam. You get a decent number of accessories, including a wifi adapter. You also get a mounting kit that will seemingly help you easily mount the camera on your handlebars (and it works very well, just takes a LONG time to tighten the thing!) and the mount will work with seemingly EVERYTHING including your pet duck...EXCEPT YOUR HELMET. You need to buy a separate mounting bracket for your helmet EVEN THOUGH THIS IS ADVERTISED AS A HELMET CAMERA!
- Having said that, the mounting bracket is metal, but the mount on the camera itself is plastic. If you're lucky, this will last you maybe ten uses before you strip the thread and have to hack in your own metal nut.

But seriously, it seems like I have more complaints than positives, but the truth is, I'm still glad I have this camera. For what I paid (which must have been a "discontinued product" price) I feel I got a really, really good deal.

HEADS-UP TO MAC USERS: To run the Mac software, you need to visit Ion's web site and download the Mac software. DO NOT RUN THE MAC SOFTWARE FROM YOUR COMPUTER: you will get error messages saying the camera isn't connected. YOU NEED TO RUN THE SOFTWARE FROM THE MEMORY CARD THAT IS IN YOUR CAMERA. product_title: Panasonic LUMIX GX7 DMC-GX7 16.0 MP Mirrorless Micro Four Thirds DSLM Camera
review_body:
I really like this camera. I purchased it to have a smaller camera that still takes high-quality RAW images for traveling. My main rig is a Canon 6D with a 24-105 lens and I really love that combo, however, it's very conspicuous and heavy which makes traveling with it challenging. In addition, I really don't want to take too much of a chance on the 6D getting stolen.

I've just done test shots in my house and on my street but, so far, I'm very happy with the results. I purchased the camera as a body only and am using the Panasonic 12 - 35 lens which gives me a 24 - 70 35mm equivalent. The lens, while small compared to a DSLR lens is still kind of big so this combo won't be as inconspicuous as I'd hoped but it takes very sharp photos and will hopefully be very versatile as a travel lens.

The RAW images can be processed by Lightroom just like I'm used to and I've configured the controls to work similarly to my 6D in that I have the AE/AF button configured for focus (not the shutter button) and I can use the front and rear dials to control aperture and shutter speed. By default the rear wheel control shutter and the front control aperture and, while I know I can customize the direction the wheels spin, I'm not sure just yet if I can switch the wheels so that the rear one controls aperture which would make it more like what I'm used to on my Canon.

But right now I can set it to use single-point focus, hold the AE/AF button down to get focus and then re-compose. The half-push of the shutter will then measure for exposure.

The built in flash is not awesome but you can tilt it up for bounce and that produced good results in my home (light colored walls with a white ceiling). To be clear, the flash can't be permanently positioned for bouncing straight up (like a speedlite). Instead you have to hold it back with your finger (it's springy) and that can be awkward as I have to position my left hand so that my finger can reach across the top, but it works and you get used to it.

The built in Electronic View Finder (EVF) works well and I've not noticed anything too weird about it as others have reported. You can see your subject clearly as well as all the control settings. I wasn't sure how much I'd use the LCD screen as I'm so used to using a view finder (I never use live view on my 6D except for the very rare times I shoot video on it) however, it's actually pretty handy. You can put your camera in a position where looking through the EVF is awkward (even if it does tilt) and use the LCD to compose and, even better, set your focus point by just touching what you want the camera to focus on. So even though I have the focus points set to the center, I can still move it around by touching the LCD screen if I want. This helps, for example, when you put the camera on the ground for a very low shot but don't want to put your head down to see the EVF. You can use the LCD to compose the shot and then touch the screen where you want focus to be. Very cool. FYI, pushing the Display button puts the focus point back into the center.

You can turn the LCD off to save battery, however, you have to cycle through various modes by pushing the display button. I have not figured out if I can customize a button to toggle the rear LCD off and of yet.

One thing to be aware of. I purchased the camera from Pixibytes through Amazon. I ordered the camera body only and separately ordered the 12 - 35 mm Panasonic lens. The box it came in was for the kit that includes the 14 - 42 lens so apparently Pixbytes opens the box, removes the kit lens, re-seals the box and then sells the body only. This is not obvious (if it's mentioned at all) on the Amazon page for the product. It seems new and all the accessories were still wrapped up in the original plastic, however, it did not come with a manual. The box does not say that a manual is included, however, un-boxing videos onYouTube seem to indicate one does. The Amazon web page says the model is the DMC-GX7SBODY, however, the box says DCM-KX7K. I'm not sure what the deal is here.YouTube seem to indicate one does. The Amazon web page says the model is the DMC-GX7SBODY, however, the box says DCM-KX7K. I'm not sure what the deal is here.

product_title: Tekoo® Wireless Bluetooth Rechargeable Handheld Monopod Cell Phones Selfie Stick Portable Extendable and Adjustable Size Phone Holder for Iphone Samsung HTC -One Button Control
review_body:
I received this as a free review sample. First, this selfie stick is one of only two brands that I have tried that can extend over two feet. Second, it easily accommodated my Galaxy Note 3 phone.

Since there are detailed product specs I will not repeat them. I have been using this stick for nearly four months and the one spec that I initially questioned - it charges up in a half hour - has proven to be accurate. Pairing and connecting via bluetooth is very easy, and since it is classified as an input device you can actually use it as a remote shudder release while streaming music to another bluetooth device. Not everyone will need that feature, but it's there.

Not only will it hold a Note 3, it will hold one encased in a thick case such as the [[ASIN:B00GOHUNO6 Galaxy Note 3 Case Fliptroniks Brown Wallet Flip Case Made With Real Leather Id and Credit Card Slots]]. It was a tight fit, and probably will always remove the Note 3 before using it with this stick, but the fact is it will fit. For bumper style cases on a Note 3 (and possible 4 and 5) there should be no problem because of the depth of the gripping arms and the strength of the holding spring.

One final feature that I like is the body is larger in diameter than many sticks and easier to hold. Plus while I would not call it waterproof, I have used it in a light drizzle and the wetness did not harm it.

Bottom line: if you need a general selfie stick there literally dozens (if not hundreds) of different ones from which to choose. However, if you need one that will extend all the way to 27 inches this and only a handful or others will meet your needs. This one is every bit as good as the other longer models that I have used and tested.

review_body:
I am not a "pro" photographer. I am strictly an amateur but hate getting ripped off.

I was looking for a battery grip for my "Canon 6D" camera primarily because I wanted the extended battery life of two installed batteries. I like to go to our local North Carolina Zoo and do a lot of "wandering around" with my camera to take pictures. I hate to run out of battery power so doubling my batteries with this "grip" was my primary goal.

The "Canon" grip was incredibly expensive compared to this (and many other) "after market" grips. I spent a lot of time reading a lot of reviews (and horror stories) about other "after market" grips and since this one seemed to get many favorable reviews for the price, I decided to gamble and give it a try. I'm very glad I did.

This grip not only extends my battery power with two batteries instead of one, it makes my camera more comfortable to use. It does add some weight and size to the camera but I do not find that unacceptable. As a matter of fact, I rather like the "feel" of the camera more with the added grip because it does provide me with extended battery life and a bit more to hold onto when using the camera.

This "Vivitar" grip seems to have all of the features of the "Canon" grip at a substantially lower cost. All the electronic functions and features of my "Canon 6D" work perfectly with this "Vivitar" grip installed. This grip allows storage of my camera battery cover as the "Canon" grip does when it is installed which is a handy feature to me. I have used "some" of the buttons on the grip and the "dial" for camera feature selections and they all seem to work perfectly. The electronic "prongs" of the grip fit in the battery compartment to the camera with no problems and the color and finish of this "Vivitar" grip match my "6D" very well in my opinion.

Installing this grip to my camera takes some care. It is a bit of a "snug" and "careful" fit as I'm sure the "Canon" grip would be too. I do take time and patience when using my stuff so I am slow and careful with the install and removal of this grip. I did notice if you "hurry", this grip can be "cocked" a bit and not fit properly but again, I suspect that would be true of any grip, including the "Canon" grip.

Overall, I am very glad I purchased this grip. It fits my "Canon 6D" very well and matches the camera well too. It is substantially cheaper than the "Canon" brand grip and I appreciate that too. Now I cannot claim that every "Vivitar" grip will work as well as this one has for me but for the saved money, I am very pleased with this purchase.

review_body:
Anyone who shoots outdoors with the Lumix DMC-LX7 camera would be wise to buy the DMW-LVF2 live, electronic viewfinder.

PROS

+ Replicates the camera's back LCD image perfectly, with 1.44M-dot equivalent, 100% field of view, and 1.4x (35mm camera equivalent 0.70x) magnification.

+ Features a 0º - 90º vertical pivot for angled viewing.

+ Can be manually switched between the camera back LCD and the LVF.

CONS

- Looks bulky and ruins the lines of the sleek, compact LX7.

- Looks and feels like plastic on its exterior surfaces, which doesn't match the appearance of the metal-bodied LX7 camera.

- The price, which I've never seen discounted off MSRP, is almost 40% the street price of the LX7 itself.

(See the attached photo for an image of an LX7-mounted LVF pivoted 90º to show the knurled diopter wheel, plus a front and back view in normal position.)

*****

The function of this LVF delivers and makes it an invaluable accessory, despite its rather steep price and a couple nitpicky appearance cons. The LX7 is a beautiful little camera with outstanding capability for its size and price, and the LVF only makes it better.

review_body:
The Kodak CFH-V15 camera is worth the money and peace of mind. There are a few quirks that knocked off a star, but overall, I was impressed.

Positives:
-Easy to setup, and install.
-Video quality is 720 with adjustable quality options in the app.
-App is easy to use and fairly intuitive.
-Gives peace of mind when away from home to monitor my puppy.
-Long power cord included to allow flexibility placing the camera.
-Night vision in low light / dark settings.
-Web page access to view when mobile app not able to be used.

Negatives:
-App uses a network port that is blocked by my works WiFi, forcing me to use mobile data or the website.
-Have to pay for more advanced options like motion activated recording.
-Expected better range of motion being able to aim the camera downward.
-When using the talk feature, speaker distorts and doesn't reproduce very accurately.

All things considered, this camera is great. I use it to monitor my puppy when left alone, and it is great for peace of mind and knowledge of what really goes on when I'm not home. If he is getting into trouble, I can talk to him and tell him to stop.

I recommend this product!

product_title: Telguard/ Telular TG-1EXPRESS (3G/4G) 3G RES COMM EXPRESS FOR 3G/ 4G
review_body:
I was able to use this device to transform an older wireless alarm system from a landline to cellular. Previously, it used old style telephone lines, then later a VOIP phone (Ooma) over my internet cable. The obvious weakness is that if the line or cable to my house was cut, it can no longer call the monitoring station. The TG-1 Express fixed that.
HOWEVER - The instructions are not user friendly for older alarm systems and/or DIY amateur installers (I had both of those situations). For example: it can be powered by two means: 1) the aux power position on your alarm system (mine doesn't have one) or 2) an AC to DC adapter. I was able to use a 12v 500mA "wall wart" (general name for those small plug-in adapters). But determining the polarity and power output needed by the TG-1 was difficult. I had to go out and buy a multi-meter to make sure I didn't fry the TG-1 when powering it up. It would have been simple enough for them to have recommended several models of compatible DC adapters. Or at least specify not only the voltage (which they did) but also the amperage (which they didn't). I had to search all over and make an educated guess.
ALSO - If the TG-1 becomes unpowered, it cannot call out. It has no battery backup of its own (they do tell you this). What they don't tell you is how to remedy that. If you use the "aux power" setting of your alarm box, you must make sure not only of its polarity, voltage and amps, but also if it is powered by your system's internal battery backup during a power failure at your house/business. To make sure the DC adapter connected to the TG-1 still works if I lose power, I bought a battery UPS backup. It took quite a lot of looking on the internet to figure out what kind I needed.
Finally - As an amateur DIY guy, I was only able to do this with advice from my alarm monitoring company (which I paid $40 for - well worth it too). I also had to call a backup battery manufacturer to make sure theirbox would work and for how long (at least 10 hours, which is plenty). That at least was free. All of this info could have been supplied in their manuals. Unfortunately, they're written for the professional installer, not the amateur.
Still, I avoided replacing my alarm central or any of its many sensors, saving about $1000. Now my connection is cellular, not land line as before. Yes, my alarm monitoring company charges more, but I think it's worth it (went from $9 per month to $22). There probably is a way to make the TG-1 Express a backup to a landline, but I don't know how to do that. I still think you get charged the higher rate anyway. IMO cellular alone is better than landline alone. Many of the newer alarm systems are cellular alone, so somebody else agrees. Hopefully, they know more than this amateur!

product_title: iShot Pro G7 Pro iPad Air 2 Tripod Mount Works with Most Cases & Sleeves Even Thick Otter Box Cases
review_body:
I bought the iShot Pro to use with my iPad Air 2 for two specific reasons: 1) to hold the iPad on a stand at the right height and angle for me to use while playing guitar, watching instructional videos or reading tablature music; and 2) to use the iPad for live video broadcasting via the Periscope app. In both cases, I attach it to my Benro tripod, which has a fantastic ball-joint head mount that works perfectly with the iShot. It might be less useful with a different tripod; fortunately I have versatile camera gear that works well with this.

The width of the iShot's crossbar support is adjustable, which gives you some latitude for adjustment with different iPad cases. My iPad is in an [[ASIN:B00QF5MXFY Anker Bluetooth Folio Keyboard Case for iPad Air 2 - Smart Case with Auto Sleep / Wake, Comfortable Keys and 6-Month Battery Life Between Charges]] - not the ideal type of case for either of these applications. However, the iShot holds it rock solid tight. With the folded over keyboard lid, it's a very tight fit in the iShot, but that's what I wanted. Once I tighten it into place, the iPad isn't going anywhere. I haven't tried it without the case or a different one yet, though, so I can't speak to how it works universally. It's solidly build but compact and very lightweight, very easy to travel with.

For guitar/music use, the application of the iShot is simple - hold the iPad at the right angle for me to see the screen comfortably while playing. When attached to the ball-head tripod, it does this wonderfully.

The same holds true for using this to livestream video from home. Set it up on the tripod, point the camera at you, get to filming. It's worth noting that (as of the time of this writing) Periscope only broadcasts in Vertical, and you need to use the Facetime camera if you want to be able to watch the video feed and respond to user comments in real time. Having the iPad in the iShot mount made this really easy, because it accommodates pretty much any angle.

The real test - and why I gave it 5-stars - was using it "in the field". I took this rig (iPad, Anker case, iShot, Benro tripod) to San Diego Comic-Con, and used it to livestream video from various outside events. I set the tripod up behind vendor tables and conducted interviews. And, feeling brave, I folded my tripod up like a monopod and hoisted the iPad up over crowds to get audience "crane" shots and views of events. I'd never have done that if I had any fear the iPad could fall out of the iShot. But the grip was so dependable, I was able to hold the tripod high at angles to get interesting views, and nothing ever slipped!The real test - and why I gave it 5-stars - was using it "in the field". product_title: Nikon MB-D16 Multi Battery Power Pack/Grip for D750
review_body:
It's got a nice heft and I can even see part of its magnesium frame by looking into the battery compartment at an unpainted portion. Also reassuring to have the peace of mind that it's a Nikon accessory on a Nikon camera body with a Nikon USA Warranty.

I've used an aftermarket grip on my D7100 in the past and have had a great (albeit short term, ie. less than one year) experience with a company called "Vello". With that, I chose to purchase another Vello grip for my D750, but this time I experienced issues with the joystick on the grip being unreliable. It was as if the joystick wasn't re-centering each time which was a nuisance. If it was consistent, I could have worked around it for the price I paid for it, but it wasn't and when it malfunction it was always a surprise at an inopportune time. However, ignoring the possibility that I got a bad sample, the Vello did weight a few grams more than the Nikon grip. I'm assuming because of extra plastic used in its construction to make it as durable as the lighter magnesium Nikon grip. That's a good thing in my eyes because I would be a little worried if the plastic Vello weighed less than the magnesium Nikon.

The command dials on the Vello grip were also much easier to spin, both front and rear dials. The Nikon grip has a very tight front dial, especially tough to spin if it's warm and your finger tips aren't absolutely dry. I'm hoping the front dial on this Nikon grip "breaks in" so to speak, and becomes easier to spin. The rear dial on the Nikon grip is a bit easier to spin, but not nearly as easy as the dial on the D750 body itself.

While both the Nikon and Vello grips have a full length reinforcing bar for the bottom tripod mount, I do feel better knowing that the Nikon has a magnesium frame vs the plastic one on the Vello (which for all I know, could be just as tough, or tougher), but I don't have the resources to test that out.

I had a completely terribleexperience with a DSTE grip I purchased here, but I won't go into that unless someone really wants to know.

Bottomline: I am not happy with the price Nikon is charging for this battery grip, and I would have been perfectly content with the Vello grip (and even strongly suggest it as the best alternative) had I not received a faulty one, or if I used it only occasionally, however I made the choice to go with Nikon because I intend on keeping this grip and the camera body for as long as possible (I am a hobbyist, not a paid professional), and I use the grip almost 95% of the time so I would rather avoid risks later down the road. I figure I spent $2k on the camera body, another $2k on a single lens, so what's another $300 for a little bit of insurance and peace of mind? I understand the fallacy in that argument, especially as a hobbyist, but when it comes to choosing tools, or other things of frequent utility, I believe in "buy once, cry once". Giving it 4 Stars because Nikon sells it for over $100 more on their own website, adding proof that it's priced to gouge you.

review_body:
This is a great security camera system for a home or small business user. Setup is a breeze, the hardest part will be running the wires, for which you might want to hire an electrician if you aren't experienced doing this.

The system is basically a small specialized computer box/DVR with a 2 TB HDD that connects to all the cameras. This box needs to have a hard wired ethernet connection to your network if you want to view the video remotely and also should be located by a display (D-Sub VGA or HDMI output from recorder box). Almost any current TV or computer monitor will connect fine.

All I had to do to get the system up and running was plug in everything and it worked right away. If you want to use your smartphone or tablet to view the video feeds you only need to scan a QR code on the monitor when running the setup wizard and it will get the Serial Number/IP of the camera and connect right away.

Video quality is excellent. I have tried some inexpensive web based systems claiming to be HD, but had such poor video quality you would never be able to identify a face from the video feed any further than a couple feet away. With the Q-See HD system the quality is good enough you could identify a face from many feet away (probably 10 or 20 feet), you would have to go to zoom/telephoto cameras to see people from further away than that, this is meant for fairly close up, like around steps of a house or in a store.

My only complaint is that the fan noise is fairly loud from the DVR, so I wouldn't put it too close to my entertainment television, and it also generates a fair bit of heat, so make sure it is in an area with some air circulation to keep it from getting too hot. Also, some of the video cables are very tight going on the DVR, you might need a pair of needle nose pliers and gently twist them the rest of the way to make sure the cable locks into place.

Night time quality is excellent, it has both a passive IR mode and an active IR mode where it illuminates some IR producing LED lights around the front of the camera. The active mode would be used at night, and the passive at dusk. Both will be displayed as black and white on the monitor/video.

product_title: iHomeSet Compact Telescope - Waterproof - Dustproof - Single Hand Focus
review_body:
iHomeSet Compact Telescope - Waterproof Dustproof - Single Hand Focus

I’ve had binoculars of the years and this is my first monocular. The quality level is the first thing you notice as you take it out of the box. It comes in a nice protective carry case. That case has room for the mini tripod that was included in my review version. I don’t think it comes with the one for sale in this listing. If you get one or buy one later it will fit in the case. You also get a soft cloth for lens cleaning and the hand grip cover you attach. I am uploading pictures which will show the hand cover attached.

The monocular itself is very well constructed. It is coated in a water resistant rubber cover. The focus and eyepiece move very smoothly. It feels absolutely great in the hand. You feel like you are holding a much more expensive item than this costs. The optics are top notch. The image in view is sharp and clear and bright and easy to focus. I love the ample distance you can focus on. I have trees outside and can easily look in on how my neighboring birds are doing. There is only one nit I can pick and it’s the string that holds the small eyepiece cover. The large cover is permanently attached by a rubber cover with a rubber leash. It’s not going anywhere for a very long time. The small one is held in place by a thin string. That string came undone and was impossible to easily reattach. I, instead, bought a lens cap tether and secured it that way. A much better solution I hope the manufacturer retrofits. I don’t want to lose the cap, now I won’t.

Overall this is a great monocular and worthy of serious consideration. Especially with the tether fix. It is a top notch device.

This product was provided at or nearly no cost for the purpose of evaluation and review.

product_title: Wonderpark 8gb Smile Face Badge Hidden Camera Realtime Mini Sd Card DVR Camcorder(include 8gb Card)
review_body:
First, I did receive this product free for testing and review. I'm hoping that my impressions and observations will prove helpful to you in your decision making. If you have questions, feel free to post them in the comments section and I'll do my best to answer based on my own experience with the camera.

What you're getting with this order:
(1) Smiley face badge camera
(1) 8 GB micro SD card
(1) USB charging cord
(1) dash mount

What is this thing, and what's it supposed to do?:
This camera, capable of 720x480 video resolution, is hidden in the left eye of a clip on smiley face button. It can be used to record video (with audio), take a photo, or solely to record audio. It also comes with a dash mount to be used in a vehicle. This requires assembly with some very small screws. An 8GB micro SD card is included with purchase and the included USB charging and data transfer cord allows you easily view and store the recorded files.

Does it work?: The short answer is yes, it does. It can do all 3 tasks it claims to be able to do. The long answer is that it can be more of a hassle than I'm looking for in this price range where more easily manipulated cameras can be had. It is difficult to know which mode you're in with this button and so if video is really important, you have to hope you're correct. I was able to get all 3 functions to work, but it definitely took some practice, and again it's a bit more work than I want to do.

Video: Power on, then hold video button (labeled in user's guide) for 3 seconds to begin filming. Hold again for 3 seconds to stop.

Photo: Power on, quick press the video/photo button (labeled in user's guide) to snap photo.

Audio only: Long press audio record button (labeled in user's guide). Press again to stop.

Positives:
-Button looks real, camera very difficult to see
-Purchase includes micro SD card
-Charges quickly and holds a charge for hours when using and months when not in use (I've had it for over 3 months and it's still got a bit of its 3 month old charge.
-Video is decent with good lighting

Negatives:
-Buttons are very small and difficult to press while button is being worn.
-Difficult to know which mode you're in and if video has started/ photo has been taken
-Video nearly worthless in low lighting situations.

Anything else of note?:
-As of the posting of this review, the camera is eligible for free shipping to members of Amazon Prime.
-Being wholly uninterested in having a happy face badge mounted on my truck's dash, I did not test the mount beyond assembling it. While it has some annoyingly small screws, it does work.

Bottom line: If you're willing to put in a little practice, this happy face badge camera might be just what you're looking for. It does perform each of its advertised functions. But it is difficult to operate while being worn, and it is difficult to know if video has been started and it would be easy to think you were recording and have no clue until you got home that you missed what you had intended to record. I'm giving it 3 stars, which to me is not a bad rating, it simply means that I think the camera is "okay". product_title: FLIR FX Dash/Sports Bundle Wireless 1080P HD Video Monitoring Security Camera
review_body:
I’ve used them all. Dropcam, Smartcam, you name it.
The FX is no doubt the best camera in the market.

What you really need to know:
* The price is fair, it’s pretty much the same as other but has much more features and abilities compared to all the other cameras.
* Video stream quality is the highest and the clearest out of all the cameras I’ve tried. You should know that this is affected by the quality of your internet connection, but I assume that the regular household at 2015 will have a good one.
* Setup is extremely easy and intuitive. Flir guys really did a great job there.
* View of multiple cameras is easy well handled, specially with the tablet version of the app. You can see multiple streams and let’s admit it - this is SUPER important for users that have more than one camera.
* RapidRecap is am amazing technology that only Flir has that enables you to review a large period of time in less than a minute, with all the movement and action superimposed on one stream. This is a mind blowing feature I show-off to to everyone. Besides the fact it’s very useful, it’s also very neat!
* Smartzones are great, enabling you to concentrate the automatic alerts only to a specific area out of all the space the camera captures.
* As just mentioned - alerts! Super important. At least if you want to know that someone just got into your house, instead of realizing it and watching the recording of someone stealing half of all you got (and I’m not talking about a divorce).
* More alerts! You can also set sound triggered alerts.
* Night vision works great. Important for feeling safer when you’re asleep.
* Access to multiple users works great, I’ve tried connecting 3 of our family members connecting to the camera in parallel and it worked great.
* Camera has an internal battery so if your power goes down it doesn’t die.
* Camera has an SD card slot that enables you to record locally,which is a HUGE benefit compared to all the other cameras around.

This is all that comes to my mind right now. I really enjoy in the FX.

Get it, trust the experienced guy.

product_title: COOLPIX L610 16MP 14x Optical Zoom 3.0-inch LCD Digital Camera NIKKOR ED Glass Lens (25-350mm) Macro Shooting, VR Image Stabilization, New Intelligent AF System, Full HD (1080p) Movie (Black) (Certified Refurbished)
review_body:
Why I bought this: My heavily researched and much-loved Canon PowerShot SX150 was stolen, and I needed a replacement fast. The Canon I loved is only available from resellers at high markups now that it is no longer produced. I settled on this Nikon as one of the few options relying on AA batteries--a must for me.

Note: The Canon camera i replaced had other features this Nikon does not, but I am setting those aside when judging this camera--this is not based on a comparison of the cameras.

The fatal flaw: The camera is slow in a number of ways that sort of baffles me in this day and age.

Toggling b/w picture-taking and picture-reviewing mode takes so long that half the time I think I have turned the camera off. Indeed, at times I do just that and turn it on to get to picture-taking mode (the default mode) more quickly.

Unlike the Canon, when pressing the shutter button slightly in order to trigger focus etc., the little "green box" that appears on the screen when ready to shoot can take a very long time, and sometimes does not appear. I can understand this happening in conditions of low light (this camera has extreme difficulty letting you take a picture in low light), but the problem occurs inexplicably at times where light is bright, subjects are motionless, etc. more than once i have missed an opportunity for a group portrait while others are snapping away and i am tapping and retapping the shutter button trying to "trick" the camera into settling on something to focus on.

I do not have problems with other features of the camera, and when I am taking pictures most of the time, its sluggishness is simply a hassle.
But this "slowness" really kills this camera's functionality under a lot of circumstances of daily living when I drag the camera to "events" or gatherings and I'd like to use it more spontaneously.

product_title: Fujinon XF 55-200mm f:3.5-4.8 R LM OIS Zoom Lens (Certified Refurbished)
review_body:
I was wanting to get the newer 50-140mm, but then I got to use one that my friend had and I changed my mind. That lens is a beast. Part of the reason I have moved away from Nikon is because of the bulk. The 50-140mm reminds me of my 70-200 f/2.8 Nikkor in size and weight. It also looks way too big on the little XT-1 and even more so on the X-T10.

I hadn't even considered the 55-200mm before because, in the Nikon world, that is one of those awful, cheap, plastic kit lenses they practically give away with their consumer cameras. Then I read an article on FujiRumors that said many of the lenses were on sale. The 55-200mm was $150 off so I decided to read up and I was very (pleasantly) surprised. All the reviews were very positive (which seems to be the case with most Fuji glass). This is a very solid and well-built metal lens. The image quality seems fantastic; it is very fast focusing with the new v.4.0 firmware update, and the OIS allows me to shoot at much slower than my old shaky hands alone can.

I'm very glad I got it and wouldn't hesitate to recommend it to anyone.

review_body: Rather than buying a new one I bought two cameras that were used.  I bought this one and a Canon si20.  I really like this camera for the run of the mill family shots that seem to comprise most of my photography.  We us and slr for the more professional landscape stuff.  This camera is light.  It almost feels toy like in construction.  The battery is special. something I am not fond of considering the canon uses regular AA batteries ,  But this battery seems to last a long time and it charges quickly on the portable charger.30 minutes and you are done.  The buttons on this camera are smooth which makes them unobtrusive and hard to find.  but they work and there are not too many.  The canon and this one have more capability than I will ever use.  I like the on line manual.  If it were paper it would be too big to carry.  The Leica lens on this camera seems to be OK.  There is some cropping and crinkling on the picture edges that is not noticeable on the canon.  But the difference is pretty small and with the mundane subject matter I use this for, (like birthdays, around the house stuff, maybe a picture of a cancelled check, etc. the distortion around the picture's edge is not even noticeable.All in all this is the better of the two I bought.  The canon is heavier, delays pictures much longer, and seems a bit more user unfriendly than this one.  I'd buy this for a kid's present or a gift for an older person who just wants a point and shoot with a little pizzazz but it is not for a serious photographer.
